en: The *Śrībhagavadbhaktirasāyana* composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī,
together with his own commentary on the first chapter (*ullāsa*), which is a most excellent work.
Chapter One.
They declare that the supreme goal of human life here is the yoga of devotion to Mukunda, whether it is conjoined with the nine aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*) or practiced alone—
a state whose nature is incomparable bliss and consciousness, untouched by suffering.
I manifest that [reality] for the complete satisfaction of all, according to the perspective of the scriptures. ||1||
I bow to that certain infant in the house of Nanda, whom Śiva worships as if he were his own eleventh [son], while his ten forms are present through the tips of his toes acting as commentaries.

At the beginning of the work, intending to ward off potential obstacles by means of auspiciousness consisting of meditation upon the Blessed One, the author—the foremost among the learned—first sets forth the subject matter, the purpose, and the connection as prerequisites for the engagement of a discerning person, stating: "The nine rasas...
[and so on]. He describes the four well-known paths to the goals of human life known as *yogas*—namely, *karmayoga*, *aṣṭāṅgayoga*, *jñānayoga*, and *bhaktiyoga*—in the verse:
"Three yogas have been taught by me, desiring the welfare of men."
Knowledge, action, and devotion—there is no other means anywhere.
Thus, by the word of the Blessed One, even the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) should be understood as being included within the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga).
"One should concentrate the mind on a single point, having mastered the breath and the posture,
remaining unwearied and sustained by the yoga of dispassion and practice."

This is also because he is instructed in these very matters. Among them: *garbhādhāna* (conception), *puṃsavana* (ensuring a male child), *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair), *jātakarman* (birth-rite), *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving), *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food), *caula* (tonsure), and *upanayana* (initiation); the four *vedavrata*s (Vedic vows); *snāna* (graduation bath) and union with a wife; the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); the seven forms of domestic sacrifice (*pākayajñasaṃsthā*)—namely, the *aṣṭakā*, *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, *śrāvaṇī*, *āgrahāyaṇī*, *caitrī*, and *āśvayujī*; and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, the *āgrayaṇa*, and the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices.

The seven forms of the *haviryajña*— namely, the *nirūḍhapaśubandha* and the *sautrāmaṇī*— and the seven forms of the *somayajña*— namely, the *agniṣṭoma*, *atyagniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, *ṣoḍaśī*, *vājapeya*, *atirātra*, and *aptoryāma*— these and other duties prescribed by the scriptures in the form of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), known as *karmayoga*, are to be practiced until the purification of the internal organ is achieved;
for one should perform these actions until one becomes weary of them,
or until faith arises in listening to My stories and so forth.
Thus, from the words of the Blessed One;

and its status as a means for purifying the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is established by such scriptural passages as: "By dharma one drives away evil; therefore they call dharma supreme," and "By whatever sacrifice, even by the *darvihoma*, one becomes indeed pure-minded."

Consequently, for one whose mind is not yet softened, there arises knowledge of reality preceded by world-weariness (*nirveda*); for one whose mind is softened, however, there arises devotion (*bhakti*) preceded by faith in the *bhāgavata-dharma* through hearing the narrations of the Lord and so forth. Thus, both are presented as the preliminary limits. Then, having practiced the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*) through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one should bring the mind to a state fit for one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), which consists of a continuous succession of cognitions having the single form of the Lord, like a stream of oil.
As it is said: "When the yogi is weary of worldly undertakings, detached, and has his senses restrained, he should, through practice, hold his mind immovably within the Self."
When the mind, being held, quickly wanders and remains unsteady, one should,
with vigilance, bring it under one's own control by means of the path of restraint.

From such words of the Blessed One, and because that [discriminative knowledge] exists, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*)—consisting of non-attachment to the body, senses, and so forth—as taught in the *Śrīmad Bhagavadgītā Upaniṣad* from the passage beginning with "humility, freedom from hypocrisy" and ending with "this is declared to be knowledge," becomes firmly established. And the limit of this yoga of knowledge is the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*).
Through the Sāṅkhya, there is the process of the reversal and following of all states of being.
One should contemplate the origin and dissolution of existence until the mind becomes serene.
The mind of a person who is disillusioned and dispassionate, and who understands what has been taught,
abandons its wickedness by reflecting upon that which has been contemplated.

One should not direct the mind toward anything else, but should remember that which is appropriate through the paths of yoga such as Yama, through the science of Ānvīkṣikī, or through the worship of my icons.
From such words of the Blessed One:
"O sage, for one who worships with the yoga of devotion as described,
all desires within the heart perish once I am established in the heart."

Thus, for a certain highly fortunate person whose mind is entirely turned away from all objects and who, through devotion to the means of practice (*sādhana-bhakti*) following the words of the Lord such as these, has established all love directed toward sense-objects solely upon the Lord; in his mental state—which is the result of all spiritual practices, which takes the form of the Lord, and which consists of a melting (*druti*) produced by hearing this work that strings together the majesty of the Lord’s qualities—that [love] is manifested in the form of *rasa* through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*).

The stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) called *rati*, taking the form of the Blessed One’s own appearance, manifests as the direct realization of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). This alone is *bhaktiyoga*; those who know aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*) call it the supreme, unsurpassed human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Therefore, for the yogin endowed with devotion to Me, neither knowledge nor dispassion is generally considered the highest good in this world.
That which is attained through ritual actions, through austerity, and through knowledge and dispassion;
through yoga, through the duty of giving, and through other means of spiritual welfare.
Through the yoga of devotion to me, my devotee easily attains everything—
whether heaven, liberation, or my own abode— if he so desires.
Indeed, my virtuous, steadfast, and single-minded devotees do not desire even liberation from rebirth,
though it be granted by me.
They say that supreme indifference is the great, unsurpassed liberation;
therefore, may there be devotion to me for one who is free from desire and indifferent to worldly aims.
For those who are single-mindedly devoted to me, for the virtuous who possess equanimity of mind and have attained supreme awakening, there are no qualities arising from virtues or faults.
Such are the scriptural statements and those who have experienced them.

For the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of all systems is that the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is happiness unmixed with suffering; as for the well-known doctrine that there are four human goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—that is merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), like saying "the plow is my livelihood," because it attributes the status of the result to the means. Therefore, the position that happiness alone is the human goal is not abandoned.

The logicians (*tārkika*) maintain that there are two human goals (*puruṣārtha*): happiness and the absence of suffering. This is not correct, because, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), one should postulate that happiness alone is the human goal. For when knowledge generates desire, its being directed toward happiness is the very limiting condition (*avacchedaka*); it is not its being directed toward either happiness or the absence of suffering, due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*). As for the absence of suffering, its utility lies solely in its serving as a defining characteristic of happiness.

However, as the authors of Nyāya treatises have suspected: once it has been stated that the absence of suffering serves a purpose only for the sake of happiness, it can likewise be argued that happiness serves a purpose for the sake of the absence of suffering, because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) alone provides the decisive criterion. For the pervasion—"when there is happiness, there is the absence of suffering"—is universally accepted, since it is observed as a concomitance (*sahacāra*) free from any limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*).

Therefore, since the absence of suffering necessarily occurs at the time of pleasure, it is logical that it serves as a defining characteristic of pleasure, because it pervades it. [Objection: One might argue that "when there is the absence of suffering, then there is pleasure," and thus it pervades it. [Reply: This is not so, because there is a deviation in cases such as deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. Therefore, since the absence of suffering does not pervade pleasure, it cannot serve as its defining characteristic. For that which is pervasive is established as being otherwise explained by its status as the cause for the existence of the pervaded.
And pleasure does not pervade the absence of suffering; therefore, pleasure itself is the independent human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

If it is argued that, since the absence of suffering is understood as having the nature of happiness (*sukha*), liberation (*mokṣa*)—which is the absence of suffering devoid of all happiness—could not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), then let one offer a final farewell to such a person! Proponents of Vedānta, however, declare its status as a human goal on the grounds that it consists of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Therefore, he states that the yoga of devotion to the Blessed One is likewise the supreme human goal precisely because it is a happiness unmixed with suffering: "It has the nature of the consciousness of incomparable bliss, untouched by suffering."

By this, all such arguments as "devotion is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is not included among dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa" are refuted. Since dharma, artha, and kāma do not possess the status of being independent human goals in themselves, and since there is both unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and a lack of universal applicability (*ananugama*) in treating only the pleasure produced by them as the human goal, it is established that—setting aside qualifiers such as "produced by dharma"—mere pleasure (*sukha*) alone is the human goal. Consequently, just like the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the bliss of devotion (*bhakti*) also possesses the status of an independent human goal.

Because it exists in proximity to liberation, it may be included within liberation; or, because it is produced by the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), it may be included within dharma. For those who are dull-witted regarding faith, it can be asserted that the bliss of devotion (*bhakti-sukha*) is included within dharma, since it is produced by the *bhāgavata-dharma*. Alternatively, because the devotee’s liberation from saṃsāra is necessary, the path of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) is included within liberation. Therefore, whether as part of the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha-catuṣṭaya*) or independently, the path of devotion is indisputably a supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), as its nature is that of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Establishing its nature as supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), he states the intermediate classification: "either combined with the nine sentiments (*navarasa*) or alone. This will be made clear further on. The term "Mukunda" indicates the objective focus (*viṣaya*) of the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*). It will be stated that the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) of all, the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*) himself, is the foundational determinative factor (*ālambanavibhāva*) for the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) of devotion. Furthermore, this constitutes the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) at the beginning of the work, according to the traditional teaching: "There is never any inauspiciousness in any undertaking for those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed One, Hari, the abode of all auspiciousness."

"I expound that" indicates the subject matter and the relationship [between the teacher and the teaching], thereby precluding the charge of being rootless from the perspective of the scripture. "For the satisfaction of all" indicates the purpose; for while the satisfaction of the virtuous is natural, the intention is that for others as well, it serves as a cause for the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) through the removal of doubt and misconception by means of the arguments set forth in this work. Who, then, are those who maintain that the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is the supreme human goal? Listen to them:
"Indeed, there is no other auspicious path for those wandering here in *saṃsāra* than this."
From which devotion to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva may arise.
If that Dharma well-practiced by men does not produce delight in the stories of Viṣvaksena, it is indeed nothing but mere exhaustion.
Indeed, devotion to Kṛṣṇa is accomplished through acts of charity, communal feasts, austerity, fire-offerings, chanting, Vedic study, self-restraint, and various other such auspicious means.
The Lord Brahmā, having contemplated with his intellect the entirety [of creation] three times, determined that; being immutable, one should find delight in the Self alone.
In this world, this alone is the source of the highest good for men:
that the mind be steadily fixed upon Me through intense yoga of devotion.
O Lord, may that liberation which embodied beings might attain through meditation upon Your lotus feet, or by hearing the accounts of Your births,
never exist even for Brahmā within his own exalted glory.
"But what [is gained] by those falling from their celestial chariots, crushed by the sword of Death? and so forth.

Here, indeed, the fact that this is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is shown directly—both by implication as the intended object of the focus on being accomplished through all meritorious deeds, and by the words "supreme bliss" (*niḥśreyasa-nirvṛti*). And in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā*:
"Of all yogis as well, he whose inner self is absorbed in Me..."
"One who possesses faith and worships Me is considered by Me to be the most disciplined," and so forth.
Now, other doctrines also teach that the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) is a means [to liberation]:
"The yoga of devotion directed toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva..."
It quickly generates dispassion and that knowledge which is without cause.
Whether free from desire or desiring all things, one of noble intellect who desires liberation should worship the Supreme Person with intense yoga of devotion.
Some, by means of exclusive devotion, having Vāsudeva as their supreme goal,
shake off all evil entirely, just as the sun dispels the mist.
And in the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā: "By devotion one comes to know Me as who I am and what I truly am;
then, having known Me in truth, one enters into Me immediately thereafter," and so forth.
In this regard, it has been clearly stated that [the means] is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in itself, as it is merely a means to something else.

To this it is replied: there is no fault, because the twofold nature of devotion (*bhakti*) is established through the distinction between the fruit and the means. For instance, by deriving the word *bhakti* from the verbal root *bhaj* (to worship) in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), the term "devotion" denotes the fruit—namely, the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) taking on the form of the Blessed Lord. And since that [fruit] constitutes the unsurpassed human goal, the authority of the previously mentioned doctrines remains unimpaired.

Likewise—by the etymological derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning "that by which the internal organ is made to possess the form of the Blessed One, that is, to be served or cultivated," the word *bhakti* denotes the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and chanting (*kīrtana*). Since these do not constitute ends-in-themselves (*puruṣārtha*), there is no contradiction in the validity of those doctrines that maintain their status as means. Just as, for example, by the etymological derivation as a state (*bhāva*), meaning "the act of cognizing" (*vijñapti*), the word *vijñāna* in the phrase "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*) refers to Brahman itself.

"Vijñāna" (consciousness) is derived from the instrumental sense (*karaṇavyutpatti*) as "that by which one cognizes"; thus, in passages such as "it extends the sacrifice," it functions as an instrument. This has been clarified by Prabuddha:
"Recalling and causing [others] to recall Hari, who removes the flood of sins, they bear their bodies with horripilation through devotion that has arisen through devotion."

In this context, the first word "bhakti" is used in the sense of an instrument (karaṇa-vyutpatti) to refer to the duties of a devotee (bhāgavata-dharma), while the second is used in the sense of a state or result (bhāva-vyutpatti) to refer to the fruit. Thus, by learning the duties of a devotee and through the devotion arising therefrom,
one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa easily crosses over the insurmountable Māyā.

Thus, in the conclusion, because the word *bhāgavatadharma* is used in place of the first term *bhakti*, one might argue as follows: "It should not be said that there is no justification for a twofold division of *bhakti* based on the distinction between the means (*sādhana*) and the fruit (*phala*). For instance, although the study of the Veda consists of grasping the syllables (*akṣara*), its fruit is indeed the grasping of those syllables; yet there is a distinction here due to whether it is dependent upon a teacher or not. Similarly, in this case too, *bhakti* in the form of *bhāgavatadharma* is the means when dependent upon a teacher, and when it has reached its culmination (*niṣṭhā*) by being independent of a teacher, it is that very same thing which becomes the fruit. [The author replies: This is not so, because in some places [the text] says: "In some places they weep from thinking of Acyuta... and so forth.
They laugh, they rejoice, they speak words beyond the world;
they dance, they sing, they practice the discipline of the Unborn; and having attained supreme bliss, they become silent.

Thus, because of the reflection on having fulfilled one's purpose in the middle [of the text]. For if devotion, produced by the duties of the Bhāgavatas, were to serve as a means toward another fruit—just as the grasping of syllables (the result of study) leads to the knowledge of meaning, its performance, and so forth—then the text would not have declared that they become satisfied and remain silent after attaining the supreme human goal; rather, it would have pointed out further duties to be performed thereafter, yet it does not point such out.

Therefore, since the twofold nature of devotion is established by the distinction between means (*sādhana*) and fruit (*phala*), it is proven that there is no contradiction anywhere among the statements regarding its being a means and the statements regarding its being a fruit, provided their respective scopes are distinguished. As for passages such as "they shake off evil entirely," this applies equally to both the means and the fruit, because it will be explained later that even devotion in its form as a fruit possesses visible results. And thus:
"For this [devotion] is the austerity of a man, or his sacred learning, or his well-performed sacrifice, or his hymn offered with a focused intellect."
The purpose defined by poets as unerring is the description of the qualities of Him whose fame is supreme.

Who would not delight in the chanting of the virtues of the One of Supreme Renown, which is pleasing to the ear and mind, which is the medicine for worldly existence, and which is sung by those whose thirst has ceased?
A person may become dispassionate without [the slaughter of] sacrificial animals.

In such passages, the statement of the means (*sādhana*) is to be construed as being for the sake of the result (*phala*), just as in the case of the mantra "mix the *matsara* with cows. For in that instance, the established meaning in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā) is that one should mix the *matsara*—the Soma juice—with milk produced from cows. And in the *Uttaratantra* (Vedānta), regarding the passage "the great, the supreme unmanifest" (*mahataḥ paramavyaktam*), it is established in the *Ānumānikādhikaraṇa* (Brahmasūtra 1.4.1–3) and specifically in the sūtra "But the subtle [body], because it is for its sake" (*sūkṣmaṃ tu tadarthatvāt*), that the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) denotes the body produced from that [Great Principle].

In this context as well, the two terms *guṇānuvarṇana* (description of qualities) and *guṇānuvāda* (reiteration of qualities) should be understood as being directed toward the joy produced by them; otherwise, they would not result in the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Now, it might be argued that elsewhere it has been stated that devotion to the Lord is identical to the knowledge of Brahman. For instance, the scripture—beginning with "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting"—establishes that the knowledge of Brahman is to be accomplished by all meritorious deeds. This was likewise determined in the *Sarvāpekṣādhikaraṇa*.

If it be argued that this commencement of inquiry is useless—since, even here, the nature of devotion to the Lord as being identical with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) has been established by the previously cited statements through the characteristic of being achievable only through all meritorious deeds, and since its status as the unsurpassed human goal has been settled by the *Catur-lakṣaṇī Mīmāṃsā* through the removal of misconceptions and contradictions—[we reply:

No, because of the difference between devotion and the knowledge of Brahman regarding their essential nature (*svarūpa*), means (*sādhana*), fruit (*phala*), and qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*). For devotion is the state of the mind taking the form of the Lord, preceded by a state of melting (*dravībhāva*), and consisting of a conceptual mental modification (*savikalpaka-vṛtti*).

Brahma-vidyā is a non-conceptual mental state whose sole object is the secondless Self, free from the state of solidification. Hearing this book, which consists of the weaving together of the majesty of the Lord’s attributes, is the means for devotion (*bhakti*). Great Vedic statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) are the means for Brahma-vidyā. The fruit of devotion is the intensity of love directed toward the Lord. The fruit of Brahma-vidyā is the cessation of ignorance, which is the root of all misfortune. All living beings possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for devotion; however, for Brahma-vidyā, the qualification belongs only to the wandering mendicant (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*) who is endowed with the fourfold means.

However, the fact that both devotion and the knowledge of Brahman are to be accomplished through all virtuous deeds such as sacrifice and charity is common to them both, just as it is for the desire for heaven and the desire for inquiry. For instance, although it is established by the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" that these sacrifices are the means to attain heaven, the sentence "the New and Full Moon sacrifices [are performed] for the sake of desires other than heaven" makes known that they also lead to other results.

Likewise, by the passage beginning with "This very [Self]... through the study of the Vedas," the fact that [the means] are instruments for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is also understood according to the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*); the same will apply to devotion (*bhakti*) and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). For the identity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) pertains to the identity of the effect, not merely to the identity of the individual causes, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus, between devotion and the knowledge of Brahman—just as between the desire for heaven and the desire to know—the relationship of being the means to a result and the absence thereof, as well as the state of being accomplished by identical means, will likewise obtain.

[Objection: But surely, if devotion (*bhakti*) were distinct from the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), it would not possess the status of the unsurpassed human goal (*puruṣārtha*), just like heaven (*svarga*) and the like. [Reply: This is not so; for while heaven and the like—being objects of enjoyment restricted to specific places, times, bodies, and senses—cannot be enjoyed everywhere, and thus lack unsurpassedness due to being permeated by the two types of suffering characterized by perishability and dependence, the stream of bliss in devotion can be enjoyed, like the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, in a manner common to all places, times, bodies, and senses.

Because it is possible [to attain], and because its unsurpassed nature is established through the absence of being permeated by the two types of suffering characterized by perishability and dependence;
as it has been said:
"Having abandoned one's own duty, [one should seek] the lotus feet of Hari..."
If one who is unripe falls while practicing devotion,
wherever he may fall, what misfortune has befallen him?
What goal was not attained by those who practiced according to their own dharma?
The wise person should strive for that very cause;
for that which is not obtained by those wandering between the high and the low— namely,
happiness— is obtained from elsewhere, just as suffering is.
In due time, it flows everywhere with profound velocity.
O dear one, a person who serves Mukunda never, under any circumstances, wanders again through the cycle of worldly existence,
as they remember the embrace of Mukunda’s feet.
One who desires to abandon people should not grasp at their flavors.
Those whose minds have been placed even once here upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, being enamored of His qualities,
do not see Yama, nor those who bear nooses, nor his soldiers.

"For they see [the results] even in their dreams once the expiation has been performed," and so forth. For this very reason, even when a transgression occurs, the qualification "untouched by suffering" (*aspṛṣṭaduḥkha*) is employed in order to demonstrate the absence of contact with pain. Consequently, there is no similarity with heaven and the like, which become insipid upon their ultimate transformation. By this, its distinction from worldly aesthetic flavors (*laukikarasa*) is also explained; for those [worldly flavors], being not prescribed by the scriptures, do not cause the destruction of sin, and thus involve contact with suffering when a transgression occurs. However, a great distinction will be stated regarding devotion (*bhakti*), because it yields both seen and unseen fruits.

If it is argued that this being the case, since detachment from the bliss of devotion would be impossible, the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) would likewise be impossible, and thus the commencement of the four-chapter *Mīmāṃsā* intended for those qualified for it would not occur—this is true. However, [the scripture] was not commenced for those attached to the bliss of devotion; rather, even for devotees, such inquiry is necessary for the purpose of determining the nature of the one to be worshipped. Furthermore, it was certainly not intended as an objection that detachment from the bliss of devotion would not occur. Indeed, it is said: "Even sages who delight in the Self and are free from worldly ties offer disinterested devotion to Hari, the One of Vast Strides, whose qualities are of such a nature."
Because, by such statements as these, devotion to the Blessed One is established even for those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta). ||1||

[This is the commentary on the first verse, which serves as a summary of all the topics to be explained: Those who have long been oppressed by the powerful disease of saṃsāra have trained themselves intensely for its pacification.
O wise ones, may you drink this elixir of devotion, which is manifold and transcends all expenditure. ||2||
Therefore, he teaches the purpose of this work by means of its title—“saṃsāra... and so forth. This is clear. ||2||
When the mental state of the mind, which has flowed forth from the Lord's dharma, has attained a continuous stream, it is designated as "devotion" (bhakti) toward the Lord of All. (3)

In order to state that devotion to the Blessed One constitutes the supreme human goal by virtue of its nature as aesthetic rasa (*rasa-rūpatā*), [the author] first declares its general definition with the words "of that which is melted" (*drutasya*). Here, "devotion to the Blessed One" (*bhagavad-dharma*) refers to hearing the qualities of the Blessed One; it is not intended to mean the performance of ritual duties (*dharma*) up to their completion out of a sense of duty. Therefore, in the statement "one should fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa by whatever means possible," the phrase "by whatever means possible" means by hearing the qualities of the Blessed One—whether performed with a sense of duty or accomplished effortlessly.

Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion [of the definition] in the case of Śiśupāla and others. When the mind—having reached a state of melting (*drava*) through hearing the qualities of the Blessed One by means of the aforementioned arousal of desire, anger, and so forth—attains a continuous flow of mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the Lord of All (which, in our view, means having the form of the Blessed One; for in our system, the meaning of the word "modification" everywhere is precisely that state of having His form), that is designated as "devotion" (*bhakti*) by those learned in the scriptures. And thus says the scripture:
"Merely by hearing my qualities, the movement of the mind toward Me, who dwell in the secret cave of all, becomes uninterrupted, just as the water of the Gaṅgā flows toward the ocean."
The characteristic of the yoga of devotion that is beyond the gunas has indeed been declared:
it is that devotion to the Supreme Person which is uncaused and uninterrupted.

Here, by the word "uninterrupted" (*avicchinnā*), a continuous flow (*dhārāvāhikatā*) is indicated. By the illustration "like the waters of the Gaṅgā," it is shown that in the case of the subject of the illustration—the mind—there is a state of fluidity. "The mental modification [residing] in me, who am the dweller in the cave of all"—this indicates the state of being the object of all. Therefore, even if a mental modification is continuous during a non-fluid state, it perishes quickly even in a fluid state; for devotion characterized by both fluidity and continuity is said not to have anything other than the Lord as its object. ||3||
For the substance of the mind is, by its very nature, solid like lac; when it comes into contact with the objects of sense as its heat-sources, it attains a state of fluidity. (4)

To clarify that very point, he describes the activity of the mind with the word "citta": for indeed, without the application of heat whose nature is burning, there is no cessation of the hardness of lac; however, it is well-established that when it comes into contact with sunlight and the like, there is merely a state of loosening, not liquefaction. In the same way, for the mind as well, there is no state of liquefaction without the conjunction of the heat consisting of the objects of desire and so forth to be described hereafter; whereas upon contact with mere objects, there is only a state of loosening. This is indicated by the inclusion of the term "heat" (tāpaka). ||4||
Desire, anger, fear, attachment, joy, grief, compassion, and so forth are the scorchers of the lacquer of the mind; therefore, their pacification is what makes it firm.

He states those very causes of affliction—beginning with "kāma" (desire). He will also explain the specific characteristics and distinctions of each of these. The meaning is that when there is an intensification of desire and the other [afflictions] toward a particular object, there is a state of melting (*dravībhāva*) of the mind toward that object; whereas when desire and the others are obscured by the shifting of attention to another object and so forth, there is indeed a state of hardness (*kāṭhinya*). ||5||

When the mind is in a state of flux, that which is projected by an object with its own form is a portion of the sound "cultivation" (bhāvanā), consisting of the existence of the latent impressions of mental formations (saṃskāra-vāsanā). //6//

He states the purpose of this liquefaction with the word "druta" (liquefied): the meaning is that it is not a quality of the self produced by a perishing cognition, as imagined by the Tārkikas and others. ||6||
The mind merely becomes slack through the absence of affliction;
therein, no object whatsoever enters as a latent impression (vāsanā). //7//

The negative particle (*nañ*) here has the sense of "slight. When the mind comes into contact with objects that are "non-afflicting"—that is, slightly afflictive, such as sunlight and the like—it undergoes only a slight dissolution of its parts. In such a mind, which has become slackened like lac, no object enters as a latent impression (*vāsanā*); rather, it enters merely as a semblance (*tad-ābhāsa*), distinguished from a true latent impression. This is the meaning. ||7||
That which has entered into a state of fluidity and subsequently attained a state of solidity does not relinquish that [solidity] even when fluidity returns once more. (8)

Regarding the statement that "when there is fluidity of the mind, there is latent impression (*vāsanā*); but when there is a state of laxity, there is only the appearance of an impression," he provides the determining factor here with the words "in the state of fluidity. Just as when a substance such as vermilion, having entered a state of fluidity, or lacquer, through the removal of its hardness, comes into contact with wood or other materials, that very substance appears as a dye; however, a dye that has entered a state of laxity does not appear in that same way.

Thus, when an object's essential nature has entered into a mind in a liquid state and remains there until the stage of solidity, that [nature] is not abandoned by the mind because it continues to manifest even when another object is grasped through a subsequent state of liquidity; therefore, this is called a *vāsanā*. However, that which has entered into a state of laxity does not persist until the stage of solidity; or, even if it were to persist, it is abandoned by the mind at the time of grasping another object, and thus it is termed a semblance of a *vāsanā*. This is the meaning.

For this very reason, it has been said that he whose mind, once liquefied, has entered into the form of the Blessed One, becomes one who has accomplished all his duties by perceiving Him at all times:
"He who sees the self as having the nature of the Blessed One in all beings,
and all beings within the self which is the Blessed One— he is the best of devotees."

Even at the time of perceiving all beings, because only the form of the Lord has entered into the state of fluidity and is thus manifest, the appearance of the Lord in all beings is established, just as in the case of lacquer and wood. And he [the Lord] is the supreme devotee (*bhāgavatottama*), because such a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is indestructible; this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, the claim that only one who knows Brahman is such [a devotee] is refuted; for since that knower of Brahman does not require the state of fluidity, he is not counted among the superior, middling, or ordinary devotees.

In this context, however, regarding the state of full maturation of the liquid condition (*dravāvasthā*), it is said that one who perceives [the Lord] in all beings is the best devotee (*bhāgavatottama*). Regarding those possessed of a slight degree of the liquid condition through the manifestation of latent impressions (*vāsanābhāsa*), it is said:
"He who maintains love, friendliness, compassion, and equanimity toward the Lord, His dependents, the ignorant, and the hostile, is a middling devotee. Thus it is stated.

This means that for one in such a state, the state of melting (dravāvasthā) is about to arise. However, for one whose mind has neither developed the state of melting nor even slightly produced it, but who instead personally practices the duties of a Bhāgavata with faith for that purpose, he is characterized by the collection of factors for the destruction of the state of hardness—namely, "He who with faith endeavors in worship to Hari alone in His image, and not toward His other devotees, is remembered as a *prākṛta-bhakta* (an ordinary devotee). Thus it is said.

*Prakṛti* means "commencement"; that which exists within it is *prākṛta*. This refers to the present performance of the means of devotion (*bhakti-sādhana*) that has been undertaken. Furthermore, this very state of melting (*dravāvasthā*) is also designated by such terms as *praṇaya*, *anurāga*, and *sneha*. As it is said:
"He whose heart does not abandon [its attachment] even when Hari himself—though addressed with words of reproach—is the destroyer of the multitude of sins."
He who holds the lotus feet [of the Lord] with the cord of affection is said to be the foremost among the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavata).

*Praṇaya* (love) is the state of fluidity (*dravāvasthā*), and that very state is the *raśanā*—the means of binding, like a rope. The meaning is that once one has entered that state of fluidity, there is no returning back out. Because the manifestation of the Lord’s essential nature (*svarūpa*) as it enters the state of fluidity is threefold, even the highest devotee (*uttamabhāgavata*) is of three types. Among these, the first is accompanied by the manifestation of the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatva-bhāna*), as for example:
"The ether, wind, fire, water, and earth;
the luminaries, living beings, the directions, trees, and so forth..."
"One should bow to the rivers, the oceans, Hari, the body, and whatever being exists, without [mental] distraction. And so forth.
By this, the first [type of devotion] is the natural (prākṛta) one; the second is accompanied by the realization of the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva-bhāna), as follows:
Therefore, this entire world is unreal in its nature, resembling a dream, devoid of foundation, and full of manifold suffering;
it exists only within you, the infinite, whose body is eternal bliss and consciousness.
That which, though arising from illusion, appears as if it were real.

By this [verse], the middle [type of devotee] is described as being superior to the Bhāgavata; the third [type] is devoid of manifestation through both modes, as follows: "As I meditated upon the lotus-feet with a mind conquered by devotion, Hari gradually took his seat within my heart, while my eyes were filled with streams of tears born of intense longing."
O Sage, with my limbs bristling with horripilation due to the overflowing of love and being utterly blissful, I was absorbed in a flood of joy and did not perceive either of the two.
By this, the supreme [attainment] belongs to the best of devotees; through the ripening of the practice of uninterrupted cultivation, there is the attainment of the supreme stage. ||8||
Therefore, by the term "permanent emotion" (sthāyibhāva), this form of the object is designated;
and when manifested, it attains the state of rasa through its nature as supreme bliss.

He states that the term *sthāyin* (permanent) is indeed used in its primary sense there, and not merely as a technical convention, because the mental form (*viṣayākāra*) that has entered into the state of liquefaction (*dravāvasthā*) is never lost: "The permanent [emotion]... It is the established rule among those who know rasa that the permanent emotion itself, manifested through the conjunction of the determinants (*vibhāva*), the consequents (*anubhāva*), and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*), attains the state of *rasa*—consisting in the direct realization of supreme bliss—once the distinction between the spectator and the actor has been obscured and it resides solely within the spectator.

As it was stated by the teacher Bharata: "The production of rasa results from the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva), the consequents (anubhāva), and the transitory mental states (vyabhicārin). Therefore, the underlying intention is that the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) is now defined in order to demonstrate that devotion (bhakti) also attains the status of rasa. ||9||
For the Blessed One is indeed the very nature of supreme bliss;
when that form enters the mind, it attains its fullness as aesthetic relish (rasa).

He establishes that the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) possesses the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) in order to justify its status as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*): "The Blessed One," he says. For it is the original object (*bimba*) itself, when perceived as residing within a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that is called the reflection (*pratibimba*). And since the Blessed One, who is supreme bliss, attains the state of aesthetic flavor by becoming the permanent emotion reflected in the mind, the fact that the flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) consists of supreme bliss is beyond dispute. Nor is there identity between the foundational emotional stimulus (*ālambanavibhāva*) and the permanent emotion; for their distinction is established in common experience through the relationship of original object and reflection, just as in the case of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the individual soul (*jīva*). ||10||
Even regarding objects such as a beloved woman, there exists a cause consisting of the mass of bliss and consciousness;
though it does not appear in the form of an effect, it remains self-luminous, yet veiled by māyā.

[Objection: If this is so, let it be granted that the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*), having the form of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), possesses the nature of supreme bliss; however, since objects such as a beloved woman—the subjects of *śṛṅgāra* and other flavors—do not possess that [nature], how can they be of the nature of supreme bliss? To this, he says: "The beloved woman, etc. For indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live.

For the Śruti passage beginning with "They go toward bliss and enter into it" establishes that Brahman, whose nature is supreme bliss, is the material cause (upādāna) of the world; this is likewise determined by the principle of the aphorism, "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]. Furthermore, every effect is observed everywhere to be non-different from its material cause, just as a jar is non-different from the clay [of which it is made].

Indeed, all this is Brahman; "all this is that which is this Self"; "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—thus it has been taught by such scriptural passages as those from the *Chāndogya* and others. Furthermore, it has been determined by the principle: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] follows from words such as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*). This being so, he states that the causes for its non-manifestation in the form of partless, blissful non-duality are the two powers of Māyā: concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). He says "the effect," etc. Even though it is not an effect, its manifestation in the form of an effect is projection (*vikṣepa*). Its natural non-manifestation in the form of partless bliss is concealment (*āvaraṇa*). As it has been said:
"That which appears without an object, yet does not appear within itself—that one should know to be the illusion (māyā) of the Self, like a reflection or like darkness. ||11||

And that Brahman, which is eternally unknown, becomes the object of knowledge when it is measured by a mental modification directed toward the beloved and so forth; this occurs for a moment through a modification established in the quality of goodness (sattva) once the veil of māyā has been removed.

To the question, "How then does that [Self] appear?", he says: "As existent" (*sad iti*). For the validity of all means of knowledge (*māna*) consists precisely in their being revealers of what was previously unknown; otherwise, even memory would incur the status of a valid means of knowledge. And that which is unknown is none other than the Self-luminous Consciousness (*caitanya*), not the insentient (*jaḍa*). This is because there is no possibility of its appearing [as something unknown], and thus there is no function of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to it.

Therefore, for cognitions whose objects are beautiful things (*kānta*) and so forth to possess validity by virtue of making known what was previously unknown, it must be stated that their object is precisely that unconditioned consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by each respective [object]; otherwise, such validity would be impossible. Thus, when the veil is removed by a sattvic, direct modification (*vṛtti*) produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [consciousness] shines as delimited by those respective objects. In reality, however, it is the consciousness that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the object consisting of supreme bliss. Furthermore, because its own unconditioned nature does not manifest, there is neither immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*) nor a collapse of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). ||12||
Therefore, that very state of being an entity (bhāvatva) is apprehended in the mind;
moreover, it attains a diminished state of aesthetic flavor (rasatā) due to its mixture with dullness (jāḍya). ||13||

What is that which is extended? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Consciousness delimited by an object itself, having attained the state of being an emotion (*bhāvatva*) by ascending upon a mental modification in its liquid state, attains the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasatā*); thus, there is no inconsistency in even worldly aesthetic flavor possessing the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). For this very reason, because it is the manifestation of the Lord—who is a dense mass of undivided consciousness and bliss—there is an absolute preponderance of bliss in the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*).

In worldly aesthetic flavor (*laukikarasa*), however, because there is no manifestation of the aspect of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*) as delimited by sense objects, bliss therein is indeed deficient. Therefore, the meaning is that the flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) alone should be cultivated, disregarding worldly flavors. ||13||
Thus, having established that aesthetic flavor (rasa) arises from a stable [self] according to the Vedānta doctrine, it is now demonstrated by resorting to the Sāṅkhya doctrine as well. ||14||
"It is established" means that it is established as rasa by means of the permanent emotion (sthāyin); this is to be supplied to complete the sense. ||14||
The qualities of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva* consist of delusion, suffering, and happiness;
*prakṛti*, which is composed of these, is the cause, and every effect is likewise composed of them. (15)

He explains this very point in order to establish it: "tamas, rajas, and sattva. For the Sāṅkhyas indeed declare as follows: "All entities have as their common primordial nature (prakṛti) pleasure, pain, and delusion, because they are perceived as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Whatever is perceived as consisting of a certain nature has that nature as its common primordial nature; for example, jars, bowls, and the like, which are perceived as consisting of clay, have clay as their common primordial nature."

There is no deviation [of the reason] due to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, because we do not admit a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists apart from its underlying causes. Furthermore, these [objects] are perceived as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*). Therefore, by means of the inference that they have a nature common to those [three], the existence of a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of pleasure and pain is established. In that regard, that which is pleasure is *sattva*; that which is pain is *rajas*; and that which is delusion or dejection is *tamas*. Thus, the fact that this [primordial nature] consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) is established.

Nor is there any difference in substance between atoms and Brahman; for in the atomic theory, since a distinction is admitted between cause and effect, and because those [atoms] are beyond the senses, no effect whatsoever is perceived as being identical with them, and thus there is a lack of evidence for atoms. This is because the inference regarding the material cause of the first effect at the time of creation, aided by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*), has as its object a single material cause—just as the inference regarding the creator of the earth and so forth has as its object a single creator.

Even if proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins) accept the non-difference between cause and effect, it is not possible for the world to be perceived as having Brahman as its essence, because it is accepted that Brahman is beyond the scope of all worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). If it is argued that Brahman, though of the nature of "Being" (sat), is indeed beyond all pramāṇas, and therefore the world is certainly perceived as having "Being" as its essence—then what is the point of this untimely frantic display? For those who count themselves among the followers of Sāṅkhya, there is the conceit that since Brahman is devoid of both universals and particulars, the existence of manifold forms is impossible. //15//
Each single object, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa),
is perceived in three forms by three persons through the differences in their own mental volitions.

[Objection: But is not the reason (hetu) unestablished for you as well, since there is the possibility of identity between internal states—namely pleasure, pain, and delusion—and external objects such as jars? Or, if such identity were possible, every object would manifest in its threefold form to every cognizer. To this he says: "consisting of the three guṇas" (triguṇa). First of all, there is no possibility of identity between the internal and the external, because it is precisely external objects that become internal by being reflected in the mind. Nor does it follow that everything would appear identically to everyone, due to the difference in the auxiliary causes consisting of the respective latent impressions (vāsanā). ||16||
To a lover, a woman appears as happiness; to her husband, she appears in the form of suffering;
and through the failure to obtain her, another experiences delusion. (17)

He illustrates this very point with the words "of the amorous woman" (*kāminyā*). For toward her husband, only the *sattva* aspect of the amorous woman predominates; toward a co-wife, however, only the *rajas* aspect predominates; and toward another man who desires her but does not obtain her, only the *tamas* aspect predominates. Consequently, pleasure, pain, and despondency arise in them respectively; thus, the establishment [of these states] is logically consistent. Even the Bhaṭṭācāryas have stated that there is a difference in perception regarding a single object due to the difference in latent impressions (*vāsanā*): "In the body of a single woman, for a wandering mendicant, a lover, and a dog..."
"A corpse," "a woman of desire," "food"—these are the three conceptual constructions. Thus [ends verse 17].
This being so, when one has entered the form of pleasure within the mind, then that [pleasure], having attained the status of a stable emotion (sthāyibhāva), becomes rasa. ||18||

He states the conclusion: "This being so. The intention is that even a state such as anger possesses a quality of bliss (*sukhamayatva*), because it results from the melting of the mind (*cittadruti*) caused by an intensification of *sattva* mixed with *rajas* and *tamas*. Since the state of melting is a property of *sattva*, and since a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) cannot exist without it, and since the quality of *sattva* consists of bliss, one might think all emotions are equally composed of bliss. However, due to the admixture of portions of *rajas* and *tamas*, a gradation must be understood; therefore, there is not an equal experience of bliss in all aesthetic flavors (*rasas*). This will be clarified further below. (18)
"But the mind has the form of a single atom and does not take on the form of the object," and so forth—such views held by others have been disregarded due to their lack of authority. (19)

Regarding this, the logicians (*tārkika*) say: "The mind (*manas*) is eternal, partless, and of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*). How can it be possible to assert that it undergoes transformation into the form of an object through the process of liquefaction, using as an example a substance with parts (*sāvayava*) such as gold? For decrease and increase are not possible for that which is partless. Therefore, the description of the aforementioned stable state (*sthāyibhāva*) is inconsistent. To this, he replies with the word "parama" (supreme). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the views of the Prābhākaras—that the mind is all-pervading (*vibhu*)—and the Buddhists—that the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) alone is the mind by virtue of being the cause of the subsequent cognition—are included.

This is the position: because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like an axe, and because it is a sense organ (*indriya*), like the eye, the mind is inferred to have a medium dimension. There is no mark (*liṅga*) whatsoever for inferring its atomicity (*aṇutva*). Nor can its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) be inferred from its being an eternal sense organ, like the ear, because its eternity is unproven; furthermore, since even ether (*ākāśa*) lacks eternity, its effect—the ear—lacks eternity all the more so.

For this very reason, since that which is produced lacks omnipresence and possesses a medium dimension, there is no deviation in the inference regarding the auditory organ. According to the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever sense-organ perceives a particular quality, that sense-organ must be composed of an element possessing that quality," just as it is established that the eye and other organs are composed of elements possessing the qualities they perceive, so too should the mind be established as being composed of the five elements possessing their respective qualities, because it perceives the qualities of the five great elements; for there is no distinction [between them].

Nor is it a distinguishing feature that heterogeneous substances do not initiate [a new substance], for we observe the production of a single cloth from heterogeneous materials such as gold threads, silk threads, and cotton threads. If one refuses to accept the composite whole (*avayavin*) in that case, then one could likewise refuse to accept it elsewhere; consequently, the composite whole would be reduced to nothingness.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the mind (*manas*) is a substance composed of the five unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcabhūta*), predominated by *sattva*, subject to contraction and expansion, transparent like the eye, capable of being struck by material objects, and equal in size to the body; for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), pleasure, pain, desire, knowledge, and so forth are admitted to have the mind as their locus, and since these are perceived as pervading the entire body, their locus—the mind—must also pervade the entire body.

Regarding the absence of atomicity, our position is equal on the point that the rule—that at one time only a single cognition is produced by all the sense organs simultaneously—is accepted by both of us. Otherwise, why would two simultaneous visual cognitions not arise? As for cognitions produced by multiple sense organs, their simultaneous production is indeed admitted, since one who eats a long piece of fried bread experiences sound, touch, color, taste, and smell simultaneously.

Since you yourself accept that the contact between the skin and the mind is a cause for all cognition on the grounds that it would otherwise be impossible to account for deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it follows that for you too, the simultaneous perception of taste and touch in a piece of molasses—which is in contact with the skin but delimited by the sense of taste—would be unavoidable. Therefore, no disagreement is possible regarding the mind as we have accepted it, which is established by *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and reasoning. As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it has been disregarded due to its utter lack of logical justification. A detailed discussion may be found in our *Vedāntakalpalatā*. (19)
"The mind, having come into contact with an object, assumes the form of that object"—this has been correctly established by both the Vedāntins and the Sāṅkhyas. (20)

Therefore, he says "it grasps" to show that the capacity of the mind—which is of a transparent nature and possesses parts—to assume the form of objects, like a mirror and so forth, as described in both the Vedānta and Sāṅkhya systems, is indeed correct because it is based on authoritative testimony (prāmāṇika). Although there is a great difference in that for the Sāṅkhyas the mind is derived from the ego (ahaṅkārika), whereas in the view of the Vedāntins it is material (bhautika), nevertheless, since their shared capacity to grasp the form of objects is the same, they are presented together as being equivalent. (20)
Just as copper poured into a mold appears to take on the likeness of that mold, so too the mind, pervading objects such as a jar, certainly arises appearing in their likeness. (21)

He cites the words of the Commentator regarding the mind’s assumption of the form of an object preceded by a state of liquefaction: "Like a crucible," etc. A *mūṣā* is a crucible used for smelting. When molten copper, having been liquefied through that [crucible], is poured into a particular mold made of clay or other materials—such as the interior of a statue—it assumes the shape of the mold situated within it, because of its fluidity.

Thus, the meaning of the verse is that the mind, liquefied by passion, hatred, and so forth, flows through the doors of the eyes and other senses; wherever it is poured, it itself assumes the form of that object. Although in this statement "liquefaction" is mentioned in a general sense, it is nevertheless established—on the strength of experience—to pertain specifically to objects such as passion and hatred; however, in their absence, there is merely a state of slackening, as was stated previously. ||21||
Or, just as light, which is a manifestor, assumes the form of that which is manifested—so too, because it manifests all objects, cognition appears in the form of those objects. (22)

The mind takes on the form of the object. He states the following inference as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this point: "Or it is like light, because it removes the obscuration residing in the object. The meaning is that if a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) did not possess the form of the object, one would not observe the removal of the obscuration residing therein. (22)
This statement of the venerable Pūjyapāda, together with its reasoning, has likewise been established by the authors of the Vārttika in this same sense. ||23||
The statement beginning with "or the manifestor" (*vyañjako vā*) and so forth belongs to the Vārttikakāras as well. The reasoning shown is of the nature of inference (*anumāna*). ||23||
The manifestation of the measure (māna) arises from the mother [cognition]; once manifested, it reaches the object of knowledge (meyam).
Then, being conjoined with that object of knowledge, it attains the appearance of the object of knowledge. ||24||

He cites another statement from the *Vārttikakāras*—beginning with "from the mother"—as follows: From the mother, that is, from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which consists of the knot of the sentient and the insentient (*sacit*), there arises the manifestation of a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) denoted by the word "measure" (*māna*), which is preceded by a state of melting and is termed "functional cognition" (*vṛttijñāna*). And that [cognition], consisting of a specific transformation produced by the "measure," proceeds through the doors of the eyes and other senses as far as objects such as jars, without abandoning the internal organ delimited by the body, just like water in a canal.

And that [unmanifested consciousness], being connected with a jar or the like, assumes the form of the jar and so forth; consequently, through the manifestation of consciousness therein, there is the perception of the jar and other objects—this is the meaning of the verse. This entire process has been explained by us in detail in the *Siddhāntabindu*. 24.
In this way, such statements should be cited repeatedly in order to establish that the mind possesses the capacity to grasp the forms of objects. (25)
"Thus" means that it is not cited here for fear of making the book too voluminous; this is the intended sense. ||25||

Therefore, while there is one woman composed of flesh and another composed of mind, although they are non-different in terms of being material, the mental one is distinguished here from the physical one. (26)

This same point was also demonstrated by Vidyāraṇyapāda on the fifteenth [chapter]. He states it under the guise of a conclusion: "Therefore, [it is] composed of flesh. The meaning is that, since there can be no cognition of difference within a single material body without a corresponding difference in the forms of the mind, [the body cannot be the self]. ||26||
In many ways—such as wife, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, daughter, or mother—and likewise for the man: son-in-law, father-in-law, son, father, and so forth. (27)

He cites the universally established cognition of difference itself—namely, "the wife"—with the word *bhāryā*. The phrase "is differentiated" (*bhidyate*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. ||27||
Even upon the destruction of the external body, that which consists of mind remains;
therefore, this alone has been determined by the wise to be the permanent [self]. (28)

Having stated the difference in nature regarding being one or many, he states another difference in nature regarding perishability and imperishability—beginning with the word "bāhya" (external). The meaning is that the mind-made [body] is indeed unobstructed. ||28||
Thus, the nature of existence has been shown in general;
however, the specific definition of each shall be stated separately. (29)

It has been stated that the mental (manomayī) state alone, because it is indestructible, is the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva). However, its specific characteristics—manifesting in the form of love, laughter, and so forth—will be explained in the subsequent chapter (ullāsa); such is the meaning. ||29||
When the mind quickly grasps the Blessed One—the omnipresent, eternal, perfect one whose nature is the bliss of awakening—what else remains? (30)

Because the form of the object that has entered into the swift mind is irreversible, he says "the Blessed One," and so forth. "Omnipresent" (*vibhu*) means pervading all places. "Eternal" (*nitya*) means pervading all times. "Full" (*pūrṇa*) means being the substratum for the delusion of all duality by virtue of its non-duality. "Consisting of consciousness and bliss" (*bodhasukhātmaka*) demonstrates that it is the unsurpassed goal of human life.

The meaning is that by swallowing up the countless forms of objects that have entered since beginningless time through such a form of the Blessed One residing in the mind, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done through the manifestation of that [Blessed One] alone. (30)
Whether firm or lax, the intellect neither grasps nor is permeated;
the wise call this "knowledge of equanimity" with respect to stones and the like. (31)

He recalls the previously stated purpose of liquefaction (*dravībhāva*) itself in order to strengthen that effort—[expressed by the word] "hard" (*kaṭhina*). A hard intellect does not grasp at all; whereas a relaxed one grasps, yet it is not permeated [by the aesthetic flavor], as was already stated before due to the absence of liquefaction. Even a slight lack of liquefaction constitutes hardness, while slight liquefaction constitutes relaxation. And that [lack of liquefaction] is to be understood from the absence of the sattvic states (*sāttvikabhāva*), which are the effects of the state of liquefaction. And those [states] are: paralysis (*stambha*), perspiration (*sveda*), horripilation (*romāñca*), breaking of the voice (*svarabheda*), and trembling (*vepathu*).
"Change of color, tears, and fainting—these eight are considered the *sāttvika* [emotions]. Thus it has been stated.
For this very reason, hardness regarding the Blessed One is described: "Alas, this heart of mine is indeed made of the essence of stone!"
When, upon hearing the names of Hari being uttered,
one is not moved to transformation—
neither tears in the eyes nor joy in the hairs of the body.
O Śiva, how could one be purified without the bristling of hair, without a melting heart,
without a stream of tears of joy, and without devotion?

Without devotion, how could the inner disposition (*āśaya*) be purified? And without the melting of the mind (*cetas*), how could there be devotion? Furthermore, it is for the purpose of understanding how a melting heart would be known without the bristling of hair (*romaharṣa*) and without tears of bliss (*ānandāśru*). The mention of tears and horripilation is indicative of other symptoms such as paralysis (*stambha*) and perspiration (*sveda*). For in the absence of this melting, the mind is not transformed. Therefore, the wise say that the knowledge of those who are like stones—having become a non-receptacle for desire, anger, and the like—is a mere intellectual knowledge that does not produce the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of equanimity.

And thus the author of the *Nyāyavārttika* has said: "That which is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to pain is precisely that which is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*). The meaning is this: attachment toward a means to pleasure is the cause of mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and aversion toward a means to pain is likewise [the cause]; however, in the absence of both of these, no impression arises because there is an absence of fluidity (*dravatva*) in the mind. For this is the secret essence of all scriptures: the attainment of the form of the Blessed Lord by the mind, preceded by the removal of its taking on the forms of objects, since the operation of all scriptures culminates in this very point through their various functions. ||31||
Therefore, the wise person should, at every moment, apply firmness toward sense objects and fluidity toward the state of the Blessed One by means of the methods prescribed in the scriptures. (32)

[Objection: Surely, the mind’s being permeated by the manifold variety of desired and undesired objects that have entered it since beginningless time is its very nature—just as coolness belongs to water, heat to fire, and mobility to the wind. Since a property cannot be destroyed while its substratum persists, how can this state be reversed? To this, he says: "Hardness... [and so forth].

Indeed, the assumption of the form of an object is not the inherent nature of the mind, because it is produced by adventitious causes. To explain: the cause for the mind assuming the form of a gross object is the contact of the senses with their objects during the waking state; the cause for assuming the form of a subtle object is the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing in the mind during dreaming; and in the absence of both these conditions, the mind becomes entirely devoid of objects, as in deep sleep. The designation of "dissolution" (*laya*) of the mind in deep sleep is intended precisely to indicate its state of being objectless.

And this has been demonstrated by the Blessed One himself, the author of the Sūtras: "Even then, because of the designation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) until dissolution (*apīti*). *Apīti* means dissolution (*laya*). The prefix *āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). Taking dissolution as the limit, there is the designation of transmigratory existence during the period prior to the dissolution of that mind; the meaning of the Sūtra is not that it exists when that dissolution has already occurred. Thus, even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because the designation of transmigratory existence persists through subsequent re-arising, there is no dissolution of the mind.

The intention [of the author] is this: as for the mention of the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*) by the commentators in the passage beginning with "What indeed is this so-called subtlety?", that is according to the view of others (*paramata*), and not in accordance with their own system (*svamata*), because it would contradict the Sūtra.

The state of the mind as having the form of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavadākāratā*), however, is natural (*svābhāvikī*). This is because that mind has as its basis *māyā*—which possesses manifold, diverse, and indefinable subtle powers that serve as its cause—and because [the Lord] is eternal, all-pervading, the inner controller (*sarvāntaryāmin*) of all, and omnipresent. Just as the filling of a jar with water and so forth is achieved through external causes, whereas its being filled with space is inherent (*svataḥ*) due to the all-pervasiveness of space, so it is here. As stated by the venerable author of the *Vārttika*: "Upon the production of a jar, its being completely filled with space occurs solely in accordance with the very nature of the substance of space, and not from any causal agent; such is the case with the states of the intellect."
"The nature of cognitions as pleasure, pain, and so forth, has for its cause merit (*dharma*) and the like;
their self-established realization of the Self is pervaded by conformity to the reality of the object.

If it is asked, "Since the mind's taking on the form of the Blessed One is innate and thus independent of causes, what is the utility of the scripture?"—understand that its purpose lies in the production of the form of the Blessed One, which is opposed to other forms. For that innate form of the Blessed One which belongs to the mind is not opposed to [the attainment of liberation], because it coexists with and is a concomitant of the assumption of objective forms.

However, the knowledge born of scripture, which at the commencement of the means appears as if indirect (*parokṣa*), gradually causes its own objective form to vanish through the process of practice; once brought to direct perception (*aparokṣatā*) by the ripening of the means, it utterly destroys that [objective form] root and branch. For this very reason it has been said:
"When one, with both forms of devotion, should cleanse the impurities of the mind born of the qualities and actions by yearning for the feet of the Lotus-navelled One..."
When that [mind] is purified, the reality of the self is perceived directly,
just as the light of the sun is seen by one with clear vision.
Just as gold, when smelted by fire, casts off its dross and regains its own true form,
so too the self, having shaken off the latent tendencies of karma—
Then, through the yoga of devotion to me, he worships me.
To the very extent that this self is polished by hearing and reciting my meritorious verses,
to that same extent one perceives the subtle reality.
Just as the eye when conjoined with ointment.
The mind of one who meditates on sense objects becomes attached to those very objects;
the mind of one who remembers me dissolves into me alone.
Therefore, abandoning improper mental preoccupation— such as that found in dreams and desires— fix your mind upon Me, permeated by My being.
This much alone has been taught as yoga by me to my disciples, Sanaka and the others:
having withdrawn the mind from everything, it is to be truly absorbed in Me.
And that was stated by the illustrious Kapiladeva:
"By means of one's own dharma, which is stainless in nature and has the signless as its sign,
and by means of intense devotion toward me, long accumulated through hearing [the scriptures]."
By means of knowledge through which reality is seen, by powerful dispassion,
by yoga conjoined with austerity, and by intense self-concentration.
In this world, Prakṛti, being burned day and night by Puruṣa,
gradually disappears like the fire-drill wood when the fire has been produced.

"Prakṛti" means its own natural state, which is the taking on of the form of objects. And in the *Haṃsagītā*: "O Lord, the mind enters into the qualities (guṇas), and the qualities enter into the mind.
How can there be a mutual abandonment between these two for one who desires liberation and wishes to cross beyond [saṃsāra]?"

Thus the Blessed One gave the answer to the question of Sanaka and the others: "Understand clearly: 'I alone am grasped by the mind, by speech, by sight, and by the other senses as well; there is nothing other than Me.'"
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the modifications of the intellect according to the qualities; the individual soul (jīva) is determined to be distinct from these, standing as their witness.
When this bond of worldly existence, which bestows the functioning of the qualities upon the self,
ceases while one is established in me, the Fourth State (Turiya), then there occurs the renunciation of the mind and its qualities.

Having become disillusioned with the bondage created by egoism, which is the inversion of one's true welfare within saṃsāra, the wise man, established in the fourth state (turya), should abandon all such thought.
As long as a person’s cognition of manifold objects is not turned back by means of reasoning,
the ignorant one remains as if dreaming even while awake, just like waking within a dream.
Since the self and other entities do not exist, the distinctions,
destinies, and causes produced by them are false, just like those seen in a dream.
He who, while awake, experiences through all his senses objects that are subject to momentary change, and who, in the dream state, perceives things similar to those,
and who withdraws them all into the heart during deep sleep— he is the One.
Through the continuity of mindfulness, one perceives the activity of the three qualities and the lord of the senses.
Having thus reflected upon the three states of the mind according to their qualities, and having determined that they were produced within me by my own *māyā*,
he severed the attachment of his heart with the sharp blade of inference and sound reasoning.
Sever all doubts and mental afflictions with the sword of wisdom.
"Thus, having dispelled the delusion of manifoldness within the Self through inquiry, one should rest with the stainless mind, having offered it to Me, who am all-pervading," and so forth.

The conclusion here is as follows: those objects which present their own forms to the mind are not distinct from the Blessed Lord, because they are superimposed upon Him. This is because all objects manifest themselves through the very form of "Being"—such as "the pot is Being," "the cloth is Being," and so forth—precisely because the Blessed Lord alone is the nature of Being. Furthermore, this is understood from the scriptural text, "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates, dissolves, and breathes in That," which teaches, like the example of clay and a pot, that everything originates solely from the Blessed Lord, abides solely in the Blessed Lord, and dissolves solely into the Blessed Lord.

Furthermore, because it is sublatable like the manifold of dreams and the like, all those [affections] cease through the manifestation of the Lord's form and become identical with His nature, since superimpositions are removable by the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This being so, every love residing in objects becomes offered to the Lord alone, because nothing other than Him manifests. And such a state was prayed for by Prahlāda:
"That love which the undiscriminating have for sense-objects, which is never-failing..."
"May she, as I remember you, never depart from my heart.

Thus, by investigating through such reasoning, one determines the Lord—the non-dual Self who is pure Being, the substratum of all, and a mass of perfect existence, consciousness, and bliss. Through this investigation into the worthlessness of even waking objects, as if they were dream-objects, there arises a great detachment known as *vaśīkāra* (mastery). This has been aphorized by the venerable Patañjali: "Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the state of mastery characterized by freedom from craving for objects perceived through sight or heard through tradition."

Indeed, fourfold detachment (*vairāgya*), existing in the relationship of means and end, is well-known from the scriptures. Among these, the first is the detachment characterized by the notion of "endeavor" (*yatamāna-saṃjñā-vairāgya*), which consists of the determination: "I shall certainly eliminate the defects of the mind even with great effort. Then, while the application of means is being performed continuously, there arises a constant vigilance—like that of a physician—at every moment, [discerning] "this many defects have now been exhausted and this many remain"; this is the second, the detachment characterized by the notion of "distinction" (*vyatireka-saṃjñā-vairāgya*).
