Thus, for one who practices the two stages at every moment, that total non-engagement of the external senses with their objects—even while latent impressions (vāsanā) still exist within the internal organ—is the third stage, known as *ekendriya-saṃjñā-vairāgya* (dispassion characterized by one-pointedness). Likewise, through the practice of these three stages, that mental state consisting of a lack of longing—which arises from the ripening of the perception of defects even when women and other such things are perceived by the senses, or when heaven and other such things are heard of in scripture—is the fourth stage, known as *vaśīkāra-saṃjñā-vairāgya* (dispassion characterized by mastery).

That [dispassion] is also twofold: the lower (*apara*) and the higher (*para*). The second was aphorized by Patañjali: "The higher is dispassion toward the *guṇas* resulting from the discernment of the *puruṣa*" (*tatparaṃ puruṣakhyāterguṇavaitṛṣṇyam*). Discernment of the *puruṣa* is self-knowledge. That which follows it—dispassion or detachment toward the *guṇas*, namely objects such as sound and so forth—is the higher or superior, because it is the nature of the fruit. Consequently, the former is the lower, because it is the nature of the means; this is the meaning. And its sign is the longing for liberation alone, independent of any other fruit, as in the case of Mucukunda: "I desire nothing other than service to your feet."

O All-pervading Lord Hari, what noble person, having propitiated You who grant liberation, would choose as a boon the bondage of the self— a boon that is more desirable even than the state of possessing nothing?
Therefore, O Lord, casting aside from all sides all blessings associated with the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva,
[behold] the supreme, stainless, qualityless, and non-dual [reality].
I go unto you, the Puruṣa who is pure consciousness alone.
Having long been afflicted here by misfortune and tormented by regrets,
with my six enemies unsated and finding no peace by any means,
I have now approached Your lotus feet, O Supreme Self, You who grant refuge to the shelterless.
O Lord, protect me who have come to you for refuge—the state that is fearless, immortal, and free from sorrow.
And since divine love does not reach its highest perfection in such a state, for that purpose the Blessed One said to him:
"Abiding by the duty of a warrior, you have slain living beings through hunting and other means;
being composed, abandon that sin by means of penance directed toward Me."
"O King, in your very next birth, having become a preeminent friend to all beings and the best of the twice-born, you shall indeed come to me alone. Thus [he spoke].

And the lower dispassion (*aparavairāgya*) was aphorized by Patañjali: "Dispassion is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from craving for objects perceived through sight or heard through scripture. Therefore, it is not the case that the highest goal is achieved at that very moment [of love], because due to the absence of supreme dispassion, there is an absence of the excellence of devotion; for it is that [supreme dispassion] alone which is the cause of having accomplished all that is to be done. The mark of supreme dispassion is indifference toward all fruits up to and including liberation, as it is said:
"This world, and likewise that world, the self moving between both, those here who follow after the self, wealth, cattle, and houses..."
Having abandoned all others and worshipping me alone, who am thus faced in every direction,
with undivided devotion, I shall carry them across beyond death.
People do not accept even the granting of *sālokya*, *sārṣṭi*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, or even oneness with Me, without My service.
Some who are devoted to service at my feet and intent on my purpose do not desire identity with me; they,
being attached to one another as devotees, [do not seek such union].
They celebrate my heroic deeds.
Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the netherworlds;
neither the perfections of yoga nor even freedom from rebirth.
Having surrendered his self to me, he desires nothing other than me.
Prahlāda said: "I am free from desire and devoted to you, while you are my master and my refuge;
otherwise, there would be no purpose for us here, just as there is none between a king and a common servant."
O Lord, I do not desire even that vast [world] anywhere where the nectar of Your lotus feet is not found.
"O you who have issued from the heart of the Great One, grant me this boon: that ten thousand ears may be produced for me."
It is certain—
that bliss which embodied beings may obtain either from meditation upon Your lotus feet or from hearing the accounts of Your deeds.
O Lord, let her not fall even from Brahman’s own glory;
rather, let her fall from a celestial chariot shaken by the sword of Death.
The Queen said: "O virtuous lady, we do not desire sovereignty, self-rule, lordship over a kingdom,
nor even the state of Virāj, the position of Brahmā, or the eternal abode of Hari."
We desire to carry upon our heads the glorious dust of the feet of this wielder of the mace, which is enriched by the fragrance of the saffron from [the breasts of] Śrī.
O Supreme One, by Your protection, Indra has been brought back; having rescued him, You have awakened that heart-lotus of his— his very home— which had been seized by the Daityas.
O Lord, alas, how much of this is seized by Time for those who desire to hear you?
For them, liberation is not highly esteemed; what else is there other than the Nārasiṃha [incarnation]?
Likewise:
"For one who has devotion to the Blessed Lord Hari, the Supreme Lord of ultimate liberation,
what is the use of the meager water in small pits compared to sporting in the ocean of nectar?"
Vṛtra—
neither the vault of heaven, nor the station of Paramaṣṭhin, nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the waters.
O Righteous One, I do not desire the perfections of yoga nor even rebirthless existence, were it to be devoid of you.

O Śruti-Yamunā, for the sake of comprehending the difficult-to-perceive reality of the Self, you have exerted yourself by circling the great ocean of nectar that is Your life-story, having assumed a physical form.
O Lord, some do not even long for liberation, having abandoned their homes through association with the flock of swans that are the lotus-feet of Your majesty.

In this manner, other cases should also be inferred. When such supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*) exists—characterized by indifference toward all fruits up to and including liberation—love for any other fruit fails to arise, and love for the Supreme Self alone, who is of the nature of supreme bliss, reaches its highest pinnacle. As it was said regarding Vṛtra:
"Like fledglings [longing] for their mother-bird, like calves afflicted by hunger for the milk of their mother-cow..."
"O lotus-eyed one, my dejected mind, like a sorrowful wife longing for her beloved who has stayed away, yearns to behold you.

For this very reason, since supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya*) is impossible without knowledge (*jñāna*), and since the highest pinnacle of love for the Blessed One is impossible without that [dispassion], one must strengthen both knowledge and dispassion for that purpose. As it has been said:
By not serving the qualities of nature,
through knowledge manifested as dispassion,
and by means of yoga and devotion offered unto Me—
He encompasses me, the inner self, here.
Through the yoga of devotion joined with knowledge and dispassion,
yogis enter the soles of my feet, which are free from fear from any quarter, for their ultimate security.
Thus, O King, for the devotee of the Lord who worships the feet of Acyuta with constant devotion, there arise devotion, detachment,
and the awakening of the Supreme.
Having reached that, he attains supreme peace directly.

For a devotee (*bhāgavata*) who practices the duties of the Lord, the sequence is as follows: first, awakening to the Lord; then, supreme detachment (*vairāgya*); and finally, devotion characterized by love (*prema*). This very point was demonstrated by the Blessed Lord to Uddhava:
"To the man of knowledge (*jñānin*), I alone am the desired object, my own self is the accepted motive, and both heaven and liberation—nothing else whatsoever—is dear apart from me."
Those perfected in knowledge and dispassion know my supreme state;
therefore, the man of knowledge is dearest to Me, for he sustains Me through knowledge.

In response to the inquiry as to what that knowledge is like, it has been stated in brief: "O Uddhava, those threefold transformations which abide in you fall within Māyā, because they do not exist at the beginning or at the end."
Since these qualities such as birth and so forth belong to this world, how could they belong to You?
That which is non-existent at the beginning and the end is likewise non-existent in the middle.

The meaning is that all that is distinct from the Blessed Lord is illusory, insubstantial, and of the nature of suffering—like a dream—due to its coming into being and passing away; therefore, it is to be abandoned. The Blessed Lord alone is the Truth, of the nature of self-luminous supreme bliss, eternal, and all-pervading; thus He is to be accepted. This very point has been stated in the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā:
"Among them, the man of knowledge, ever-steadfast and single-mindedly devoted, excels.
For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me."
All these are indeed noble, but the man of knowledge alone is My very Self; this is My opinion.
For he, being disciplined in mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
"At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, Vāsudeva, as all—such a great-souled one is very rare.

This means that nothing other than Vāsudeva is real, because everything else is illusory (māyika); and Vāsudeva alone, being the Self, is the most beloved reality. Furthermore, detachment preceded by such knowledge is demonstrated:
Through the fourfold means of knowledge— scripture, direct perception, tradition, and inference—
he becomes detached from conceptual construction due to the instability found within these means of valid cognition.
Because actions are subject to transformation, everything up to the realm of Brahmā (Āviriñci) is inauspicious;
therefore, the wise man should perceive it as perishable, even though he has not yet seen its end.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"One should observe the reversal of results for men who, acting in pairs, undertake actions for the sake of destroying suffering and attaining happiness."

What joy can there be in wealth that causes constant suffering and is as difficult to obtain as one's own death, or in houses, children, relatives, and cattle, all of which are unstable even when acquired?
Thus one should know the next world to be perishable and fashioned by karma,
characterized by equality, excellence, and destruction, just like the case of those who rule over mandalas.
In response to the inquiry as to what kind of devotion toward the Blessed One arises for one who practices the Lord's dharma, preceded by knowledge and dispassion, it is said:
"If you are unable to hold the mind steady upon Brahman,
perform all actions for Me with detachment."
Full of faith, listening to my stories which are most auspicious and purify the worlds,
he sang, recollected [my deeds], and repeatedly enacted my life and actions.
O Uddhava, by practicing virtue, desire, and wealth for my sake and taking refuge in me,
one attains unwavering devotion to me, the eternal.
Likewise:
"O sinless one, I have already spoken of the yoga of devotion to you who were pleased;
I shall speak again of the supreme cause of my devotion."
May there be constant faith in my nectar-like discourse, the perpetual chanting of my praises,
steadfastness in worship, and the singing of hymns of praise unto me.
Respectful service with all one's limbs, prostration,
and regarding my devotees as superior to all beings while maintaining the thought that they are myself.
Movement of the limbs for my sake, praising my virtues with speech,
dedication of the mind to me, and the renunciation of all desires.
The renunciation of wealth and the abandonment of enjoyments and pleasures for my sake;
whatever has been sacrificed, given, offered in the fire, chanted, or whatever vow and austerity have been performed for my sake.
Thus, through these means, O Uddhava, devotion to me arises in those human beings who have surrendered their very selves; what other goal remains for them?
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:

"Therefore, one who desires to know the highest good should take refuge in a Guru who is well-versed in the word of scripture (śabda) and in the supreme Brahman, and who is established in tranquility."
There, one should learn the duties of a devotee of the Lord, regarding the guru as oneself and as a deity;
for by following them without guile, the Self, the giver of the self, namely Hari, will be pleased.
From the very beginning, one should maintain total non-attachment of the mind toward all things, while cultivating virtuous attachment toward the righteous;
and one should truly practice compassion, friendliness, and humility toward all beings as is appropriate.
Purity, austerity, endurance, silence, self-study,
uprightness, celibacy, non-violence, and equanimity toward the pairs of opposites.
Everywhere, one should perceive the Self and the Lord; [one should cultivate] liberation, homelessness, clothing made of secluded rags, and contentment with whatever comes by chance.
Faith in the scripture of the Bhagavata, as well as non-censure toward other teachings;
the restraint of mind, speech, and action; truthfulness; and both tranquility and self-control.
Listening to and chanting the names of Hari, whose deeds are wondrous, meditating upon Him,
and performing all one's activities for His sake— these involve reflecting on His births, deeds, and qualities.
Whatever has been sacrificed, given, practiced as austerity, or recited as prayer; whatever conduct is dear to oneself;
one’s wife, children, home, and even one’s life—all this is the offering to another.
Thus, one should cultivate friendship toward those who have Kṛṣṇa as their soul and their lord,
and likewise offer service to both the great and the virtuous among men.
The mutual recounting of the purifying glory of the Blessed One,
mutual delight, mutual satisfaction, and mutual withdrawal of the self [from worldly objects].
Remembering and causing one another to remember Hari, who removes the multitude of sins,
they bear their bodies with horripilation through the devotion that has arisen within them.
In some places they weep with thoughts of Acyuta; in some places they laugh, rejoice, and speak words beyond this world;
they dance, sing, and practice the discipline of the Unborn.
But having reached the supreme state, they become silent and utterly tranquil.
"Thus, by learning the Bhāgavata dharmas with devotion arising therefrom,
one who is intent on Nārāyaṇa easily crosses over the insurmountable Māyā.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should achieve purity of mind through such scriptural means as these.
I shall briefly describe those means as they were described by Nārada in the first book, according to the classification of the divisions of the earth. (33)

He promises to explain the scriptural means alone, categorized according to the different stages (*bhūmikā*), for the sake of facilitating the understanding of people; this is stated in the verse beginning with "The means" (*upāyā*). This is clear. ||33||
First, service to the great ones; then, becoming a vessel for their compassion;
then, faith in their teachings; and thereafter, hearing of the qualities of Hari. (34)
Then follows the arising of the sprout of delight, the subsequent attainment of its own nature, the increase of love, and finally, its pervasive manifestation in supreme bliss. (35)
The state of devotion (bhakti-bhūmikā) is thus described as the culmination of the Lord's qualities within oneself, and the highest pinnacle of love for Him. (36)
He states those very points beginning with "first" and so forth. As it is told in the dialogue between Vyāsa and Nārada, [Vyāsa said] to Nārada:
"O Sage, in a past life, I was the daughter of a certain woman who followed the Vedas."
The boy alone was appointed by the yogins who were about to enter the rainy season retreat to attend upon them.

Although they maintained an equal vision toward me— toward this child whose every fickleness had vanished, who was self-restrained, who held no toys, and who was compliant— they nevertheless showed compassion.
O sages, [this applies] to one who is desirous of hearing and speaks little.
Having been permitted by the twice-born, I ate once the remnants of their food smeared upon my lips; thus, with my mind purified, I was freed from all sin.
For one who proceeds in this manner, the heart becomes pure.
That very dharma alone gives rise to a personal inclination toward the self.
There, day after day, I listened with favor to the captivating stories of Kṛṣṇa as they were being sung;
and I listened to them with faith, following every word.
O dear one, it was pleasing to my mind.
At that time, O Mahāmati, my mind— steadfast and devoted to the Auspiciously Renowned One (Priyaśravas), in whom I had found delight—
perceived this world as being like a dream or an illusion, neither existent nor non-existent.
Behold me, the Supreme Brahman, in whom all is imagined.
Thus, as I constantly heard the stainless glory of Hari being proclaimed by high-souled sages during the seasons of autumn and the rainy season, [my mind became fixed upon Him].
Devotion, which removes the passion and darkness of one whose self is engaged [in worldly activity].
To me, who am thus devoted, humble, free from sin,
faithful, simple-minded, self-controlled, and obedient—
That knowledge which is most secret was declared by the Blessed One himself;
out of compassion for those who are distressed, he graciously imparted it to me as I was about to depart.
By that very means by which I learned of the power of the illusion of the Blessed Vāsudeva, the Creator, I shall go to that state where they go.
O Brahmin, this has been indicated as the remedy for the threefold suffering:
that action performed toward the Lord, the Blessed One, who is Brahman, is itself infused with Brahman.
O you of noble vows, whatever disease arises among living beings,
that very substance which caused the illness does not purify itself even when treated by medicine.
Thus, all the ritual actions of men are causes of worldly existence;
yet when conceived in another way, those very same actions lead to the destruction of the self.
Whatever action is performed here for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One,
that knowledge indeed depends upon it, being conjoined with the yoga of devotion.
Where, repeatedly performing their duties according to the instruction of the Blessed One,
they chant the qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa and remember him.
Oṃ, salutations to you, the Blessed One; we meditate upon Vāsudeva.
Salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṅkarṣaṇa as well.
Thus, by means of the designation of forms, that person who worships the Lord of Sacrifice— both with form as the mantra-body and without form— is one who possesses right vision.
O Brahmin, having understood this my own city as established by me,
Keśava granted me knowledge, sovereignty, and devotion toward himself.

Service to the great (mahatsevā) is twofold: service to the devotees of the Blessed One and direct service to the Blessed One himself. Of these, the first is as follows: "They say that service to the great is the door to liberation, while association with those attached to women is the door to darkness."
Those who are great, whose minds are equanimous, who are tranquil, free from resentment, and who are virtuous friends— they are truly noble.
Or those who have placed their affection and purpose in me,
the Lord, rather than in people who merely subsist by nourishing their bodies,
or in homes filled with the aging of wives and children.
Nor are they endowed with joy or possessed of all their needs in this world.
As it is said:
"The wise know attachment to be an unaging fetter for the self;
that very same [attachment], when directed toward the virtuous, becomes the opened door to liberation."
Patient, compassionate, a friend to all embodied beings,
having no enemies, peaceful, virtuous, and adorned with goodness.
Those who practice firm devotion toward me with undivided intent,
having renounced their actions for my sake and abandoned their own kinsmen and relatives;
They listen to and speak pleasant stories concerning me;
various afflictions do not torment these whose minds are absorbed in me.
O virtuous lady, these [sages] are truly holy and free from all attachments;
you should seek association with them, for they indeed remove the defects of attachment.
For example:
"O Sūta, the waters of the celestial river, when touched and followed in their course, immediately purify those sages who have taken refuge at whose feet they flow toward tranquility."
We do not weigh even a fraction of heaven or liberation against the company of those who attend upon the Blessed One; how much less, then, would we consider any worldly blessings for mortals?
For example:
"A human body is difficult for embodied beings to obtain, being as fleeting as a moment;
even so, I consider the sight of the Beloved of Vaikuṇṭha to be difficult to attain."
Therefore, O sinless one, we ask you about absolute security;
for in this cycle of existence, even half a moment of association with the virtuous is a treasure for human beings.
As it is said:
"Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor even dharma restrains me;
neither Vedic study, austerity, renunciation, nor sacrifices, charitable works, nor ritual fees [restrain me]."
Just as one attains vows, sacrifices, Vedic meters, sacred fords, observances, and restraints,
so too does one attain association with the virtuous, which indeed removes all attachments— [therefore, seek] me.
For by association with the virtuous, the Daityas, Yātudhānas,
beasts, birds, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas [attain excellence].
Among humans, the Vidyādharas— whose natures consist of rajas and tamas— take women who are Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or of the lowest castes in each respective age.
Many have attained my state, such as Tvaṣṭra, Kāyādha, and others;
direct service to the Blessed One is as follows:
Vṛṣaparvan, Bali, Bāṇa, Maya, and then Vibhīṣaṇa.
Sugrīva, Hanumān, the bear, Gaja, the vulture, the merchant, the hunter, Kubjā, the cowherd women in Vraja, the wives of the sacrificers, and others likewise.
They have not studied the multitude of revealed scriptures, nor have they served the great-souled ones;
they have neither observed vows nor performed austerities, yet through my grace, they have attained me.
Indeed, by their mere devotion, the cowherd women, the cows, the trees, the deer,
and others who were of deluded intellect— even the serpents and the Siddhas— easily attained Me.
That which one might not attain even with great effort through yoga, Sāṅkhya, charity, vows, austerity, sacrifices, exposition, study, or renunciation— [that state is attained by devotion].

Desiring me, those women who did not know my true nature took me—the Supreme Brahman—to be a lover, a mere paramour; yet through that very union, they attained hundreds of thousands of [liberated] selves.
Therefore, O Uddhava, casting aside both injunction and counter-injunction,
as well as engagement and withdrawal, and what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard;
Go for refuge to me alone, the Self of all embodied beings, with your whole being; through me, you shall indeed be free from fear from every quarter.

Thus, the essential point here is this: without either the company of the Lord or the company of those who are devoted to the Lord, as appropriate to one's capacity, devotion to the Lord does not arise. However, there is this distinction: because those who have attained their goal through the company of the Lord’s devotees have no further need for other associations; thus, the two kinds of service to the great ones (*mahat-sevā*) have been explained. Being a fit recipient of their compassion is the result. The compassion of those great ones toward their own object arises through their own excellent character and other virtues. And those virtues were stated by the Lord: "One who is compassionate, who does not bear malice, and who is patient toward all embodied beings."
Its essence is truth, its nature is irreproachable, and it is equally beneficial to all.
One whose intellect is unassailed by desires, who is self-controlled, gentle, pure, and possesses nothing;
who is free from longing, moderate in eating, peaceful, steadfast, and has taken refuge in me—such a sage [should be approached].
He is vigilant, profound in nature, steadfast, and has conquered the six internal enemies; he is free from pride yet bestows honor, capable, friendly, compassionate, and wise.
Likewise:
"One should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), and occasionally the observances (niyamas);
one should worship a Guru who knows Me, who is peaceful, tranquil, and whose very self is I."
Free from pride and envy, skillful, devoid of possessiveness, firm in friendship, unhurried, desirous of knowing the truth, free from malice, and of unfailing speech.
"Remaining indifferent toward wife, children, home, fields, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth, seeing oneself as equal in all these things, as if they were mere objects," and so on.
An example is Prahlāda, as follows:
That lord of the Daityas had four most wonderful sons; among them, Prahlāda was the greatest, for he was a devotee of Mahat through his virtues.
Devoted to Brahman, perfected in virtue, true to his word, and having conquered his senses;
he was the most excellent friend and beloved to all beings, regarding them as himself.

One who views the feet of the Noble Ones as humble as servants, who is as affectionate toward the lowly as a father, who is as loving toward equals as a brother, and who perceives his teachers as the Lord; one who is rich in learning, wealth, beauty, and noble birth, yet remains free from the arrogance of pride.
One whose mind is undisturbed in calamities, who is free from longing for what is heard or seen, who perceives the unreal in all qualities,
and who always keeps the senses, vital breaths, body, and intellect subdued;
With his desires stilled, he, free from the asuras, [conquered] the asura.

However, in the absence of such qualities in a disciple, even the attainment of the company of the Great One (mahattama) becomes fruitless; thus, being a fit recipient for His compassion constitutes the second stage (*bhūmikā*). That [stage] is also twofold: independent of one's own effort and dependent upon it. Regarding the first, for example: "Then, as he was emerging from that lake with his followers, the foremost of the immortals was being praised by the attendants of the gods."
Beholding him, who resembled a mass of molten gold, with a blue throat and three eyes,
his face radiant with grace, they bowed down, their curiosity aroused.
The Blessed One, who removes the suffering of those who seek refuge and is affectionate toward righteousness,
being pleased, spoke with joy to those who were themselves pleased, who knew the Dharma and were perfected in virtue.
Śrī Rudra said:
"O sons, you are seated upon the altar; your intended purpose is known to me. For the sake of bestowing grace upon you—may it be well with you—I have thus granted you this vision."

But he who has taken refuge in the Blessed Vāsudeva, who is beyond even the supreme velocity of that which is directly called the individual soul (jīva) consisting of the three qualities— he indeed is dear to me.
A person who is steadfast in his own duty for a hundred births attains the state of Viriñca; thereafter, he reaches me, the pervasive,
the unmanifest, the devotee of the Lord, and the follower of Viṣṇu.
O wise ones, I shall describe the state at the end of the kalpa.
Now, you are as dear to me as the Blessed Lord himself;
indeed, there is never anyone else more dear to me than my devotees.
This should be recited in solitude; it is purifying, supremely auspicious, and brings about the highest good. Listen, as I shall speak of it to you.
Thus, with a heart full of compassion and devoted to Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed One spoke these auspicious words to the princes who stood with palms joined in reverence.

In such passages as the dialogue between Rudra and Pracetas, or as in the verse, "O child, while I am free from all fickleness," there is a dependence on one’s own effort. For example, in the dialogue between Dhruva and Nārada, Dhruva said:

"This very tranquility (*śama*), which is difficult for those like us to perceive, has been shown out of compassion by the Blessed One for the sake of men whose minds are afflicted by pleasure and pain."
Moreover, although I am undisciplined and have resorted to the terrible conduct of a warrior, it does not take root in my heart, which has been pierced by the arrows of Suruci’s harsh words.
O Brahmin, tell me the path for one desiring to conquer the supreme station in the three worlds— a path not traversed by our ancestors nor by any others.
Surely you are one born from the body of the Blessed One, who, like the Sun, dances while playing the lute for the welfare of the world, piercing the Supreme Lord with your song.
Maitreya said: Having heard what was thus spoken, the blessed Nārada then,
out of compassion, replied with virtuous words to that boy who was pleased.
Nārada said:
"The path to your ultimate liberation has been pointed out by your mother;
worship that Blessed One, Vāsudeva, with a devoted soul."
Whoever desires for themselves the supreme good known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, for them there is indeed only one cause in this regard: the service of Hari’s feet.
Therefore, dear child, go— may prosperity be yours— to the pure bank of the Yamunā,
to the meritorious Madhuvana, where the presence of Hari is eternal.

Then there is faith (*śraddhā*) in those teachings. For one who possesses the previously mentioned qualities and serves the Great Teacher, faith arises toward those teachings in the form of a specific inclination, thinking: "By practicing such teachings, I too shall become one who has accomplished his purpose. As it has been said:
"Who would not take delight in the discourse of that wise man, by meditating upon whose teachings the learned sever the bondage of the knot of karma?"
O brahmins, through service to the great, by attending upon sacred fords, and by devotion to Vāsudeva, one who possesses faith shall develop a longing for the stories of Vāsudeva.
Knowledge is that wherein the cycle of waves of the qualities has ceased;
or it is the serenity of the self, as well as non-attachment toward the qualities; furthermore, it is the path esteemed for liberation, namely the yoga of devotion.

"Who that is liberated would not take delight in the stories of Hari? and so forth. The term "stories of Hari" (*harikathā*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all other duties of a devotee (*bhāgavata-dharma*). As Brahmā said:
"O Lord, may I possess that great fortune..."
Whether in this world or in another, may I be born among the animals so that, even as a single being,
I may serve the sprout-like feet of Your Majesty.

In this context, "service at the feet" is mentioned; other [means] should likewise be inferred. And this faith, increasing through the ripening of the spiritual means (*sādhana*), generates a distaste for all worldly and otherworldly objects; like hunger, it brings about a person whose sole refuge is whatever may be eaten and whose only livelihood is the practice of the Lord’s dharma—just as in the case of Parīkṣit:

"This hunger, though extremely difficult to endure, does not afflict me, even though I have abandoned water, because I am drinking the nectar of the stories of Hari falling from the lotus of Your mouth."
From such passages as these. Or, for example, as in the case of butchers and the like:
"This sun, rising and setting, indeed takes away the life of men;
yet that moment of his which has been spent in conversation concerning the One of Excellent Praise (Uttamaśloka) is truly not lost."
O Sūta, when others do not hear the sequence and progression of the bile [in the body] within the ear-cavity of a man,
his tongue becomes as false as a female frog.
And he does not sing the verse of the Wide-Strider.
Even if his head were adorned with a crown of fine cloth, he would not bow it to Mukunda;
nor do his two infant hands perform worship.
Or the two shimmering golden bracelets of Hari.
The eyes of those men who do not behold the marks of Viṣṇu are like peacock feathers;
the feet of such men share the fate of being born as trees.
Those two [feet] of Hari do not follow after fields.

A mortal who does not ever obtain the dust from the feet of a devotee of the Lord, even while living, is like a corpse; such is the case for a person regarding the Tulasī plant, which is the very footstep of Śrī Viṣṇu.
But he who, though breathing, does not perceive the scent, is a corpse.
Alas, this heart must be made of the essence of stone,
since it does not undergo transformation even when the names of Hari are grasped; for if there were any transformation, [it would surely change].
"Water in the eyes and horripilation on the body," and so forth.

However, some who are devoid of faith and intent upon the enjoyment of sense objects, while others—out of pride in their learning and the like—are intent upon censuring the devotion to the Blessed Lord, become truly contemptible even in hell. Regarding the first type, for example: "Those who do not go [to hell] because of the practice or narration of the deeds of the Destroyer of Sin..."
Alas, those who listen to evil talk concerning other realms—
which destroys the intellect and whose essence has been seized by men of ruined fortune— cast themselves into various refugeless darknesses when that talk is heard.
Do not trees live? Do not bellows breathe?
And do not other animals in the village eat and urinate?

"A man who has never brought the name of the elder brother of Gada to his ears is praised as a beast equal to a dog, a village pig, a camel, or a donkey," and so forth. [This refers to one] intent on censuring the devotees of the Blessed One, such as:

From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of Puruṣa, the four castes— the Brāhmaṇas and the others— were born together with the stages of life (āśramas), distinguished by their respective qualities (guṇas).
Those who do not worship this Puruṣa, the manifest Lord who is the source of their own selves, and who instead despise him, fall to the lowest state, fallen from their station.
Those who keep the stories of Hari at a distance, those who keep the chanting of Acyuta’s glories far away, women, and Śūdras and the like— they are objects of compassion for those such as you.
Driven by passion, those of terrible resolve, lustful, wrathful like serpents,
hypocritical, and arrogant sinners mock those who are dear to Acyuta.
In their homes, they speak to one another while attending to women devoted to sexual pleasure;
they perform sacrifices without the prescribed distribution of food and without offering ritual fees.
Those who do not know this kill animals solely for the sake of their livelihood.
Those whose intellects are blinded by pride born of wealth, power, noble lineage, learning, renunciation, beauty, strength, and deeds— even the lords [are not spared].
Being mindful, they despise the wicked who are enemies of those dear to Hari.
The ignorant do not hear that the Self— the desired Lord, praised in the Vedas— is eternally established within all embodied beings, just as space [pervades everything].
They speak of their desires as mere rumors.
Having abandoned their homes, children, friends, and wives— all created by the illusory power (māyā) of the Self—
those who turn their backs on Vāsudeva enter into darkness against their will.

Hari, who is dear to those whose wealth is their own self and who are devoid of riches, does not partake in the sacrifice of the evil-minded; nor does he favor those who are intoxicated by the pride of learning,
wealth, lineage, and ritual action.
They commit evil against those virtuous ones who possess nothing.
In this manner, other points should also be inferred. Therefore, faith in the Dharma of the Blessed One constitutes the third stage (*bhūmikā*).
Following that comes the hearing of Hari’s qualities, as follows:
"Thus, for the sake of protecting His own path, the Supreme One..."

Desiring to follow in the footsteps of this Supreme Lord of the Yadus, one should hear of His deeds— which, though performed as playful pastimes of His body, are yet imitations suited to that [human condition] and serve to grind away all karma.
O Mukunda, by that [devotion] which increases through the hearing, chanting, and contemplation of Your glorious stories,
a mortal attains that abode which is liberation from the flow of insurmountable Time (Kṛtānta).
Even the kings went from the village to the forest for her sake.
For one who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, which is exceedingly difficult to traverse,
there is no other raft than the service of the nectar of the stories of the divine sports of the Blessed One, the Supreme Person.
It shall belong to a person who is afflicted by the forest fire of manifold sufferings.

Who would not take delight in the chanting of the virtues of the One of Excellent Renown, which is pleasing to the ear and mind, which is the medicine for worldly existence, and which is sung by those whose thirst has ceased?
A man may become dispassionate even without killing an animal.
O King, what person possessed of sense would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda,
which are worshipped by the best of the immortals and from which death comes from every side?
And that vessel is disclosed:
"Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet, worshipping, bowing down, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender unto Viṣṇu."
If devotion characterized by these nine marks is truly offered to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu by a person,
then I consider that study to be supreme.
That same point is summarized:
Therefore, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign who is the Self of all, Hari, should be heard, glorified, and remembered by one who desires freedom from fear.
The examples in sequence are as follows: one who, having fallen, stumbled, or been afflicted, or having sneezed,
utters "Salutation to Hari" loudly while helpless, is liberated from all sins.
When the Blessed One of infinite power is praised,
his majesty as heard [in scripture] enters the minds of men and utterly shakes away their misfortune.
Just as darkness [is dispelled] by the sun, or as a cloud [is dispersed] by a strong wind.
Those words are indeed false and unreal,
for they do not speak of the Blessed One Adhokṣaja;
that alone is truth, and that alone is auspiciousness.
That very merit arises from the qualities of the Blessed One.
That alone is delightful, beautiful, ever-new; that alone is the perpetual great festival for the mind;
that alone is the drying up of the ocean of sorrow for men.
That which is sung as the highest fame and glory of the world.
Never should one recite that speech of Hari’s which, though adorned with variegated words, proclaims His glory— the purifier of the world—
yet is frequented by crows rather than by swans.
For wherever Acyuta is, there indeed are the stainless holy ones.
That utterance of his, even when he was not composing verse by verse, was a deluge that swept away the sins of the people;
for it was marked by the names and the glory of the Infinite One.
The virtuous listen to it, sing it, and praise it.
Even the stainless knowledge of liberation (*naiṣkarmya*), when devoid of devotion to Acyuta, does not shine, even if it be pure;
how much less so that which is eternally inauspicious toward the Lord?
For even an action that is unsurpassed does not bear fruit if it is not dedicated [to the goal].
Another person’s exertion is directed solely toward fame and fortune,
toward the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life, and toward austerity, sacred learning, and the like;
whereas my own is the non-forgetfulness of the lotus feet of Śrīdhara.
Through such means as hearing the praise of his virtues and showing reverence.
It prevents the forgetting of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet,
destroys all that is inauspicious, and spreads auspiciousness; it brings about the purification of the mind and devotion to the Supreme Self.
And knowledge is conjoined with discernment and dispassion.

Remember the lotus feet of the Teacher of the World, which grant even one’s own self; how much more so the objects of wealth and desire, which are not otherwise so highly prized, to those who devote themselves to him?
Your pair of feet, which grant liberation to the people, has been beheld;
they are meditated upon in the hearts of Brahmā and others of profound wisdom,
and serve as the supporting hand for those fallen into the well of saṃsāra.
I move about meditating; favor me so that mindfulness may arise.
Therefore, instruct me in that means by which the remembrance of your lotus feet may not cease, even for those wandering here in this cycle of existence.
Therefore, having abandoned the home— the wheel of worldly existence which is rooted in passion, attachment, dejection, anger, pride, longing, fear, and wretchedness— [one should go forth].
Worship the feet of Nṛsiṃha, which are free from fear from any quarter.
"Aha! What auspicious deed have these men performed,
or has Hari himself become pleased with them,
that they have obtained birth among humans in the field of Bhārata?"
For my longing is indeed for that which serves as a means to the service of Mukunda.
What can be said of the ascetic merit of those women who, with love and the mindset of a wife, served the Teacher of the World by massaging his feet and other such attentions?
My sacrifice is threefold: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed;
one should worship me according to whichever of these three rites is desired.
Thus, by worshipping through the paths of both Vedic and Tantric ritual action,
a person attains from Me the desired perfection in both worlds.
By offering water at his feet and performing even a simple worship with blades of dūrvā grass for one of honest intellect,
a person attains the highest state throughout the three worlds.
How could one who has given with an undaunted mind fall into distress?
O Lord of excellent renown, O best of gods, if you consider the words spoken by me to be false,
I shall act so that they may become true and not a deception.
Place your own third foot upon my head.
Therefore, observing your compassion while experiencing the ripening of my own past deeds,
I offer you salutations with my heart, speech, and body.
He who lives in the state of liberation is the heir to that portion.
Today my inauspiciousness has perished and my existence has become fruitful,
since I bow to the Blessed One’s lotus feet, which are the object of meditation for yogis.
Whether fallen, stumbling, distressed,
or even involuntarily uttering "Haraye namaḥ" after sneezing, one is liberated from all sins by chanting it aloud.
O Lord, we bow with our intellect, senses, vital breaths, mind, and speech to Your lotus feet,
which are contemplated within the heart by those endowed with devotion.
Those seeking liberation have cast off the heavy burden consisting of ritual action.
And in the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā: "Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me."
What remains for those who are servants of Him, by the mere hearing of whose name a person becomes stainless, other than His state of being the one whose feet are the sacred ford?
O Acyuta, O friend of all, what wonder is there in this that you have made yourself one with your servants who have no other refuge?
He who, though himself the Lord of lords, chose to dwell together with deer— how much more so would he do so for his devotees!
Whose footstool was pressed by the edge of his glorious crown.
Whatever one performs entirely for the sake of another— whether by body, speech, mind, the senses, or the intellect— is due to the nature that has been followed.
One should then dedicate it with the words, "To Nārāyaṇa."
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for the cowherds and the inhabitants of Vraja, whose friend is the eternal, perfect Brahman, the supreme bliss!
Thus, for the virtuous who have attained servitude to the Supreme Deity through the experience of the bliss of Brahman,
He appears as a human child to those who are still dependent on *māyā*.
They sported together with her who had accumulated a multitude of merits.
When a mortal has renounced all actions and offered himself, desiring to act for my sake, then,
attaining immortality—
And it is indeed suitable for me to become his very self.
That which is called the "trivarga"— consisting of dharma, artha, and kāma— namely,
the fourfold inquiry (īkṣā), the three Vedas (trayī), statesmanship and self-restraint (naya-dama), and the various means of livelihood (vārtā)—
I consider all of this to be the truth of the Veda.
The offering of one's own self to the Supreme Person, who is one's own true friend.
O King, he who has with his whole being taken refuge in that worthy refuge is no longer a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, men, or ancestors.
Having abandoned Mukunda, he has gone to Kartavirya.

Therefore, by performing the *bhāgavata-dharma* in this manner according to one's capacity, the fourth stage (*bhūmikā*) arises. This tetrad is indeed the means (*sādhana*). From that follows the sprouting of the seed of *rati*. *Rati*—which will be described as a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the form of the Lord entering the softened mind—is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of devotion. That alone is the sprout of the seed consisting of the performance of the *bhāgavata-dharma*. As it has been said:
"From association with the virtuous, there arises the knowledge of my power..."
They tell a story that is a nectar for the heart and ears;
from the enjoyment of that, faith, delight, and devotion will follow in succession on the path to liberation.

Faith [leads] to the experience of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of devotion; from that, the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) called *rati*; and from that, it will gradually attain the state of being the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) itself—this is the meaning.
Thus, the mind, under the influence of karma, is employed while ignorance is being superimposed upon the Self.
As long as there is no love for me, Vāsudeva,
one is not liberated from the bondage of the body.
When liberation from worldly existence occurs for a person wandering in saṃsāra, O Acyuta, then there is association with the virtuous;
and when there is association with the virtuous, then indeed there is the state of the righteous.
Toward you, the Lord of the high and the low, devotion arises in the mind.
O Lord of Madhu, may my mind, which has no other object, truly bring you delight again and again,
just as the Ganges brings her flood to the ocean.
Driven here and there by their own actions according to the will of the Lord,
they find no delight in auspicious rites, in charity, or in the Lord Kṛṣṇa.

And this fifth stage is the nature of devotion (*bhakti*). From a particular maturation of this very [devotion], there arises another sixth stage which is the fruit. This is the attainment of the essential nature; it is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as being distinct from the two bodies, the gross and the subtle. Otherwise, even if attachment were produced, it would not be sustained due to the distraction caused by the body, senses, and so forth. As it has been said: "Knowledge for the sake of the supreme good is the vision of the Self for the person."
I shall describe that which you have asked, which severs the knot of the heart.
The self is beginningless, the Puruṣa, beyond the qualities of Prakṛti;
it is the inner abode, self-luminous, by whom the entire universe is pervaded.
He, by his mere whim and as if in sport, accepted that subtle, divine, all-pervading Prakṛti composed of the Guṇas, which had approached him of its own accord.
Beholding Prakṛti, who creates offspring of various forms endowed with diverse qualities,
he was instantly deluded here by the secret of knowledge.
Thus, through a false identification with another, the person (puruṣa) imagines agency within himself while actions are being performed by the qualities (guṇas) of primordial nature (prakṛti).

Thus, for this Lord— who is a non-doer, a witness, and whose nature is bliss— there arises transmigration, bondage, and dependence brought about by that [agency], even though he himself is not the agent.
Likewise: "The Self is eternal, immutable, pure, one, the knower of the field,
the substratum, changeless, the cause of self-perception, all-pervading, unattached, and unenveloped."
By means of these twelve characteristics of the Self,
the wise man should abandon the unreal notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, which arises from delusion.

Thus, when the referent (*lakṣya*) of the word *tvam* is understood as pure, there arises the knowledge of non-difference with the referent of the word *tat*. This too has been stated: "Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves;
for the welfare of the world, He appears here through *māyā* as if possessing a body," and so forth.
And it has been shown that such knowledge occurs subsequent to devotion:
"Devotion-yoga directed toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva quickly generates dispassion and that knowledge which is without cause."
O Lord, for those who cast aside devotion to Your glorious fame and toil only for the sake of attaining pure consciousness,
nothing remains for them but that very labor.
"Nothing else, just as for those who thresh coarse husks," and so forth.

When such knowledge of reality exists, due to the firmness of dispassion (*vairāgya*), there is an increase in love for the Blessed One; this is the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*), as follows: "Like a child who has laid aside his toys, [the yogi] remains like one insentient through being absorbed in that [Blessed One]."
His self seized by the black planet, he does not perceive the world as it truly is.
Whether sitting, wandering, eating, lying down, drinking,
or speaking, he did not perceive these activities while embraced by Govinda.
In one place Vaikuṇṭha weeps, his consciousness clouded by anxiety;
in another he laughs, and in yet another he sings aloud out of joy born of that very anxiety.
In one place he cried out in longing; in another, he danced without shame;
in yet another, absorbed in contemplation of Him, he became one with Him and imitated His very nature.
In some places, he sits silently with his hair standing on end, blissful from physical touch, his eyes closed like lotuses in the water of the joy of motionless love.
By repeatedly cultivating supreme bliss for himself through service to the lotus feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown—
a service obtained through association with those who possess nothing—
He manifested that highest contentment.
He brought peace to the mind of the wretched Dumsaṅga.
He spoke thus to Prahlāda:
"In this very way— by those who have conquered the six internal enemies—
is devotion toward the Lord Vāsudeva, the Blessed One, cultivated, through which one attains delight."
When, having heard of his incomparable deeds, virtues,
and heroic exploits performed through his playful incarnations, one’s hair stands on end with excessive joy and one’s voice becomes choked with tears;
With intense longing, he sings aloud, cries out, and dances.
When, as if seized by a planet, he laughs at times, wails, meditates, or bows down to people;
sighing repeatedly, he says: "O Hari, Lord of the World!"
With the thought "I am Nārāyaṇa," he was devoid of shame.
Then the person, with all bonds released,
having burned away the latent tendencies along with their seeds by means of that great [knowledge], possesses an intention and form that imitate the state of being that [Brahman].
Having approached Adhokṣaja through the practice of devotion.
The wise know that the attainment of Adhokṣaja here for the embodied soul of impure nature— which destroys the wheel of saṃsāra—
is the bliss of liberation in Brahman.
Therefore, worship the Lord of the Heart within your own hearts.

In this manner, other stages should also be inferred. The practice of the means (*sādhana*) extends only up to the seventh stage. Beyond that, however, the fourfold stage (*bhūmikā*) is accomplished without effort.

Then there is its manifestation. The eighth stage is caused by the intensity of love for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Blessed One, who has become the object of that love. As it has been said: "Some do not desire identity with me."
Those devotees who, delighting in service to my feet and intent on my will,
associate with one another and celebrate my heroic deeds;
O Mother, those who have a serene countenance and reddish eyes behold my beautiful, divine, boon-bestowing forms as I abide here.
Together they utter a speech that is desirable.
By those lovely limbs, by their noble playfulness, smiles, glances, and charming speech,
their hearts were captivated and their very lives were taken; thus, devotion [arose].
Though I do not desire it, destiny impels me toward this narrow path.
In this manner, other [examples] should also be inferred. Thus, there is steadfastness in the dharma of the Blessed One, as stated in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"O Blessed One, the highly fortunate one who has fixed his mind upon the Śālagrāma..."
O Maitreya, he dwelt for a long time with that lord of the earth.
Among those possessed of virtues, he was the best in all virtues beginning with non-violence;
he also attained the highest limit in the restraint of his mind.
O Lord of Sacrifice, Acyuta, Govinda, Mādhava, Ānanda, Keśava,
Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva— salutations be unto You!
Thus King Bharata spoke only the names of Hari;
O Maitreya, he uttered nothing else even in his dreams.
He thought of nothing other than this state and its meaning.
The ascetic practitioner of yoga, free from attachment, performed the gathering of fuel, flowers, and *kuśa* grass for the sake of divine rites; he performed no other actions.

The lord of the earth [addressed] Bharata. And in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata: "Ambarīṣa, having obtained the great-souled earth consisting of the seven continents, as well as imperishable prosperity and incomparable power upon the earth..."
The wise man considers all that which is praised in dreams to be extremely difficult for men to attain; for when a person enters into darkness, he attains the extinction of worldly existence.
Having attained the supreme state toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva and toward His virtuous devotees,
by which this entire universe is regarded as being like a clod of earth.
He indeed directs his mind toward the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa,
his speech toward the description of the qualities of Vaikuṇṭha,
and his hands toward the cleaning of Hari’s temple and other such tasks.
He composed the Śruti for the purpose of bringing forth the excellent stories of Acyuta.
May my two eyes behold the temples and the sacred emblems of Mukunda; may my body come into contact with the limbs of His servants;
and may my sense of smell experience the fragrance of His lotus feet.
The tongue of the glorious Tulasī was offered to him.
My feet are for crawling upon the ground of Hari’s sacred field; my head is for bowing at the feet of Hṛṣīkeśa;
and my desire is for servitude, not for the pursuit of selfish desires.
Just as those who take refuge in the one of supreme fame find delight.
Thus, always performing the entire aggregate of ritual acts within the Supreme Lord Adhokṣaja, who is the object of sacrifice and the Self of all,
while establishing this earth [in its proper state],...
He indeed instructed that which was declared by the brahmins devoted to it.
Or rather:
"May the wise ones and the divine Gaṅgā receive him with a steadfast mind as he approaches the Lord."
Let either a Brahmin-possessed spirit or the deceptive Takṣaka bite me;
simply sing the songs of Viṣṇu!
And may there be ever-increasing delight in the Blessed One, who is infinite, and attachment to those great beings who are his refuge,
in whatever creation I may enter.
May there be loving-kindness toward all; salutations to the twice-born.
Thus the king,
possessed of firm resolve, sat facing north on ancient kusha grass at the root of a tree on the southern bank.
Upon his daughter-in-law, the wife of the ocean, he had placed the burden of his sons.
While King Parīkṣit,
that god among men, was thus seated in the fast unto death, the hosts of gods in heaven [were moved].
Having praised him on the ground, they scattered flowers with joy, and the drums resounded repeatedly.
Or as it is said:
"O Great Yogin, we who wander here upon the paths of karma shall cross over that darkness difficult to traverse by means of your news and those who belong to you."
May we conquer your illusory power, O Dāsīs who eat the remnants of those adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments enjoyed by you.

In this manner, other points should also be inferred. Devotion to the Lord’s dharma preceded by the *prayanta* [stage] is the means (*sādhana*). However, when devotion to the Lord’s dharma is established in itself, it becomes the fruit, the ninth stage (*bhūmikā*).
Therefore, there is the possession of those qualities within oneself, as follows: "Now, behold that majesty of me, the wielder of *māyā*..."
They do not crave the eightfold sovereignty that has come to them,
nor do they long for the auspicious fortune of the Supreme Lord;
rather, they attain these blessings in the world for the sake of others.
Never shall those who hold me as their supreme Self, whose form is peace, perish; nor shall my unblinking eye consume them with its flame, for to them I am both beloved and a son.
A friend [is like] a teacher, a well-wisher, and a beloved deity.

Thus, the manifestation of qualities equal to those of the imperishable Blessed One occurs on the tenth stage; it is the supreme pinnacle of love, characterized by an inability to endure separation even at the cost of one's life— as when the cowherd women experienced supreme bliss at the sight of Govinda.
For those women, a single moment spent apart from him was like a hundred ages.
When you wander through the forest during the day, an absence of even a moment seems like an eon to those who do not behold you—
your beautiful face and your curling locks of hair.
The dull-witted man gazed at her, who was looking back at him with eyes that cast glances through the lashes.
O lotus-eyed one, whenever you depart for the Kurus or the Madhus out of a desire to see your friends,
even a single moment there would be equal to ten million years.
O Acyuta, you are like the sun to our eyes when it has set.
Certain gopīs who had entered inside the house and were unable to find an exit,
with their eyes closed, meditated upon Kṛṣṇa while absorbed in thoughts of him.
Her impurities were shaken off by the intense suffering of separation from her beloved Dumsaha;
her auspicious merits were exhausted by the bliss of embracing Acyuta, attained through meditative concentration.
Even though she had united with that very Supreme Self through the thought of him being her lover,
she immediately cast off her body composed of the gunas, her bonds having been utterly destroyed.
And so forth. Only a mere indication has been given here; this will, however, be illustrated in detail in the following chapter. Thus, the discussion on *prema* (divine love) is concluded. 3436.

The characteristics of devotion to the Blessed One, its means together with their logical justification, its stages, and its essential nature have been described here according to my understanding. (37)

Thus ends the section titled "The General Description of Devotion" in the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*, composed by the illustrious Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the eminent ascetic and preeminent teacher among the wandering paramahaṃsa mendicants, who is world-renowned and independent in all philosophical systems.

Thus ends the first chapter of the *Śrī-Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*, composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī— the preeminent wandering ascetic (parivrājaka) teacher, world-renowned, and independent master of all philosophical systems— along with its excellent commentary composed by those same eminent ascetics.
The Second Chapter:
That state of being fixed in the form of Govinda which has entered the agitated heart is designated as devotion (bhakti); its specific distinctions are now being described. (1)
Devotion differs according to the differences among the causes that melt the mind;
those causes have been mentioned briefly, and shall now be explained clearly. (2)
Granted that there is a desire for a specific relationship with the body;
that [desire] would be twofold, distinguished by proximity and non-proximity. (3)

The state of being fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa that arises in the mind during the exhilaration produced by that [love] becomes, in due order, the two forms of *rati* known as union (*sambhoga*) and separation (*viprayoga*). ||4||
However, the blazing of the mind caused by anger and envy occurs;
when that [blazing] is in a state of melting, it is designated by the term "hatred" (dveṣa). ||5||
In this context, mental agitation arises from seeing that which causes distress;
it is twofold: for the purpose of destroying that which causes distress, and for the purpose of pleasing it. (6)
Among these, the first is indeed hatred, while the second bears the name of passion;
both of these shall be clarified by me further below. (7)

When there is a lack of delight in a swift movement produced by that [fear], which arises from a state of mental agitation caused by one's own faults and rooted in hatred—that state is called fear (bhaya). ||8||

Affection directed toward children and others, characterized by the relationship of the protected and the protector, as well as the other [type], the relationship of the served and the server—this too is said by the wise to be threefold. (9)
Others have declared that there is another [state] which is a mixture of service to the Blessed One and friendship;
it is that state of the form of Kṛṣṇa within the mind, characterized by the melting born thereof. (10)
Through the relationship of the protected and the protector, that [love] becomes the affection of tenderness (vatsalarati);
through the relationship of the served and the server, it is described as the love of endearment (preyaratī). ||11||
Joy is said to be the exultation of the mind, and it is of four kinds;
one consists of supreme bliss, arising from the majesty of the venerable Lord. (12)
The pure love (rati) directed toward Govinda arises from that [bhakti];
for it is held in the scriptures that the traditional account of the means of attainment (sādhana) extends only up to this point. (13)
Another [type of laughter] is produced by speech, dress, gestures, and so forth that have been altered by shame;
when there is a dilation of the mind resulting from the quickness (druti) born thereof, it is called *hāsa* (laughter). (14)
The highest wonder is born from the sight of a transcendent and marvelous object; it is considered to be the expansion of the mind within the melting state produced by that [sight]. (15)
From the onset of battle, there arises in heroes a supreme state;
from that, the expansion of the mind is called "impetuous enthusiasm" (druta-utsāha). //16//
That afflicted state which arises in the mind born from the separation from a beloved, and the attachment that is fixed upon the flow produced by that [state], is called sorrow (śoka). (17)
Compassion (dayā) is a sense of pity preceded by the knowledge of the worthlessness of the object;
when the mind is moved by that, a threefold loathing (jugupsā) arises. (18)
That which concerns putrid sores and the like causes agitation in the wise; that which concerns ghosts and the like arising from cremation grounds becomes a source of terror. (19)
Purified disgust (*ghṛṇā*), which is preceded by an investigation into the suffering inherent in the body, the senses, and so forth, is proclaimed as *jugupsā* (disgust) by the poets. (20)

But when there is an engagement out of compassion for the sake of protecting the pitiable, by that [engagement], when the mind is stirred, it is remembered by the wise as the arousal of pity (dayotsāha). //21//
That great effort of one with a swift mind, who says, "Ask for even my entire possession," is called the enthusiasm for giving. (22)
Likewise, through that most diligent application toward the protection of one's own dharma, there arises an expansion of the mind and an impetus for dharma within one's swift progress. ||23||
The dispassion known as "mastery" consists of a state of non-longing for desires;
by means of that, the tranquility of the melted mind is called "illumination. (24)
Otherwise, no movement of the mind is found anywhere;
and in the absence of that [movement], there is no other state whatsoever that can be defined. (25)
Indeed, as many as there are fleeting mental states (druti) in the mind, so many permanent moods (sthāyin) attain the state of rasa by relying upon the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors. 26.
Zeal for the Dharma, zeal for compassion, and the three kinds of revulsion lead to tranquility;
yet even these six are not objects [of attachment], for they do not have the Blessed One as their object. (27)

The hero of righteousness, the hero of compassion, the hero of the repulsive, and the hero of tranquility—these do not become "sentiments" (rasas) because they lack the quality of having distinct substrata. ||28||
Even envy and hatred directed toward the Blessed One do not attain the status of devotional rasa, for they are directly opposed to the flow [of devotion]. (29)

In that [context], a pure Furious Rasa (raudra-rasa), as well as the Terrifying (bhayānaka) and the Furious-Terrifying (raudra-bhayānaka), should not be relished by a wise person, even slightly, because it is contrary to joy. (30)
The two delights born of desire, sorrow, joy, fear, wonder, as well as enthusiasm in battle and in giving—these have the Blessed One as their object. (31)
Just as milk and water attain a state of mixture, so too do the aesthetic flavors (bhakti-rasa) when combined with the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors. //32//
The erotic, the pathetic, the comic, as well as the pleasant, the fearful, the marvelous, the heroic in battle, and the heroic in generosity—these are mixed together. (33)

Pure love (*śuddhā-rati*), the love of affection (*vatsala-rati*), and the love of endearment (*preya-rati*)—this triad is called unmixed love (*amiśrā-rati*) because it is not interspersed with other emotional states (*bhāva*). ||34||
Pure, affectionate, and beloved—these are the three varieties of the rasa of devotion;
when unmixed with other rasas, they become fully perfected. (35)
Even when mixed with others, the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is the most powerful of all;
indeed, it is in this very sentiment that the degrees of intensity and extreme intensity are observed in sexual passion (rati).
Some are purely mixed, some are mixed and combined, some are purely combined, and others are pure; thus they are of four kinds. (37)
In that regard, there are the purely unmixed [rasas]: the Furious, the Furious-Terrible;
the Heroic of Dharma, the Heroic of Generosity, the Disgusting, and also the Peaceful. (38)

Those [devotions] directed toward other objects are declared to be "mixed" (miśra), while those directed toward the Blessed Lord are known as "purely mixed" (kevala-miśrita) and "intermingled-mixed" (saṅkīrṇa-miśrita). ||39||
The three pure [types of devotion] have been described as before; they are not mixed with anything else.
Having thus defined devotion, it is now stated again in brief. (40)
It is of the nature of passion (rājasī), of darkness (tāmasī), pure goodness (śuddhasāttvikī), and mixed (miśritā).
One arises from envy and hatred, while another arises from fear and hatred. (41)
That [laughter] born of joy arises from pure *sattva*, while the other [types] arise from desire, grief, and so forth.
However, since all [eight types] are born of *sattva*, the distinction between them is made by the other *guṇas*. 42.
In that state, pleasure does not reach you at all because it is opposed to bliss;
yet you two supreme fluids partake of the very word "pleasure," for they consist of bliss. 43.
This fourfold devotion, though directed toward the Lord, becomes threefold according to whether its fruit is seen, unseen, or both. (44)
Rājasic and tāmasic devotion yield only unseen results;
mixed devotion is held to yield both seen and unseen results. (45)

Thus, although she arises from pure beings, for practitioners such as ourselves she yields fruit merely upon being seen; but for perfected ones such as Sanaka and others, she does so [even more]. (46)
Devotion to the manifestation of bliss yields both seen and unseen fruits, even more so than ritual injunctions;
it is like the act of bathing in the Gaṅgā for one whose body is withered by the heat of summer.
For one who is overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, the perceived portion [of karma] is obstructed, just as for one afflicted by cold and wind; however, the unperceived portion is not diminished. (48)
In the same way, for those liberated while living, no portion of unseen karma remains,
just as there is none for those who have already bathed and eaten and are merely playing in the Ganges.
The fruit obtainable in the present body is declared to be "seen" (dṛṣṭa); that which is to be experienced in a future body is called "unseen" (adṛṣṭa). //50//
When rajas and tamas predominate, the manifestation of pleasure is like that of a lamp-flame tossed by a violent wind; it flickers as if unreal. //51//
Therefore, although the continuum of consciousness is self-luminous and consists of the form of bliss,
it does not become the locus for the manifestation of happiness due to the influence of obstructing factors.
The mental state of the King of Cedi, which was characterized by a portion of powerful passion mixed with envy and hatred, did not lead to happiness even in the supreme bliss.
Due to the influence of a portion of his powerful nature, Kaṃsa’s mental state—mixed with fear and hatred—found no pleasure in the supreme bliss [of the Lord]. (54)
But when the obstacles have been removed in their future body, that very melting of the mind attains the state of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of devotion. ||55||
Even now, those such as the Pāśupatas who worship him out of hatred—
for them too, the result would be exactly like this, or else they would be equal to Vena.
When there is melting of the body, there may be something;
but when there is no melting of the mind, there is nothing at all—not even the slightest trace of a vein (veṇa). //57//
But that cognition which is free from rajas and tamas and has the Blessed Lord as its object is designated as "attachment" (rati) because it manifests happiness. (58)
It is reached through the progressive elimination of passion and ignorance;
for even when the practice of the means is equal, there is still a gradation in the resulting delight.
The pleasure that is seen is of the same nature as the suffering experienced in separation;
for a distinction will indeed be stated based on its being mild, moderate, or intense. (60)
In Vaikuṇṭha, Dvārakā, and likewise in the glorious Vṛndāvana,
that [devotion] is respectively mild-intense, medium-intense, and intensely intense.
This [superimposition] arises from nature, from association, from analogy, and from internal application;
it likewise stands upon the basis of conjunction and conceit. (62)
In the case of touch, sound, form, taste, and smell, whether taken individually or combined, that [cognition] occurs there; thus, each one becomes sixfold. (63)
Furthermore, this [devotion] is of two kinds: pure and mixed.
Among these, that which is without limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is pure, while that which possesses limiting adjuncts is said to be mixed.
Free from all limiting adjuncts (anupādhi) and solely grounded in the majesty of supreme bliss,
she is said to be of one uniform nature due to the infinity of her worshipful qualities.
The state characterized by fear regarding the connection with sensual desires is threefold when accompanied by limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
however, through the conjunction of the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, it becomes the rasa of pure devotion (śuddha-bhakti-rasa). ||66||
Devotion mixed with the erotic sentiment is considered devotion born of desire;
the love born of relationship attains the status of rasa, as previously described, through the union of both.
One [form of devotion] called *vatsala-bhakti* (parental affection), another *preya-bhakti* (dear-to-the-heart devotion),
and *bhaya-jā-rati* (fear-born attachment) preside over the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) known as *prīti-bhayānaka* (the terrifyingly delightful).
If these four types of delight were manifest at one and the same time, then there would be a supreme flavor, according to the analogy of the juice of a blended drink. (69)
The differentiation of rasa arises from the distinctions among individual instances of one, two, or more rasas;
therefore, one should practice that [differentiation] in some cases regarding the four types of love (rati). 70.
And the fourfold joy was clearly seen among the goddesses of Vraja;
by taking them as the object of one's mind, one's own mind becomes like that. ||71||
Devotion to the Blessed One, when intermingled with the excitants and other factors of another rasa, attains a different state of rasa, like a variegated painting. (72)

But when it is devoid of the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors of another rasa, it possesses its own essential nature and attains a tenth state of "rasa-hood" that is superior, like that of Sanaka and others. //73//

It has been stated by those expert in rasa that love directed toward objects such as gods and so forth, as well as transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) and the "exalted" (ūrjita), are not called rasa. (74)
Because it exists among the gods and because it manifests supreme bliss, that [bliss] should be applied to the Supreme Self whose nature is supreme bliss, and not to the individual soul. ||75||

Or, as for those aesthetic flavors (rasa) directed toward objects such as beloved women and the like, such a state of being rasa is not fully developed therein, because they lack contact with complete bliss. ||76||
The Blessed One’s delight in sublime flavors is more powerful than [any] minor flavors, just as the radiance of the sun is more powerful than fireflies. //77//
Anger, grief, fear, and the like, which are directly opposed to pleasure, are likewise accepted as aesthetic flavors (rasas) solely on the basis of their being experienced. (78)
Why is this rasa, which is established here by direct experience and is a thousandfold [in intensity], suddenly denied by you as if you were an insentient being? (79)

In the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*, composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī— the preeminent teacher among the wandering ascetics of the highest order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācāryavarya*), world-renowned, and independent in all philosophical systems (*sarvatantra-svatantra*)— this is the section titled "The Description of the Specific Types of Devotion."
The Third Chapter: The Second Illumination.
Now, what indeed is this thing called "rasa," and upon what does it depend?
What is its signifier, and what kind of cognition is it? (1)

The permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), when manifested as pleasure through the determinants (*vibhāvas*), the consequents (*anubhāvas*), and even the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*), is known as aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). ||2||
Since bliss is the very nature of the self, no substratum for it exists; however, there is a mental modification that manifests it toward the minds of the spectators. ||3||
The permanent emotions (sthāyins) such as love (rati) and the rest, when residing in the object of the action, are worldly;
however, when they reside in the cognizer of that [object]—even if they are similar to those [worldly ones]—they are otherworldly (alaukika).

Those things which, according to their respective natures, are the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth, when they reside in the object of awakening (the world), become, when they reside in the awakener (the Buddha), solely the cause of pure happiness for all. (5)

Therefore, the status of compassion and the other [emotions] as aesthetic flavors (rasa) is not contradicted, because it is certain that these mental states, which reside in the cognizer, are causes of suffering. ||6||
In that regard, the worldly cause of worldly pleasure and so forth, as presented in poetry, is called the *vibhāva*. (7)
Whatever effect of worldly passion and so forth is observed in the world, when it is presented in poetry, that becomes the locus for the term "enjoyment" (anubhāva). (8)
Those states of worldly pleasure and the like which serve as auxiliary factors when demonstrated in poetry are called transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). ||9||
The triad combined together should be known as the cause for the awakening of the extraordinary rasa, such as love, in the spectator. (10)
Because they are known through their relationship to themselves and others by way of a common nature, all three of these entities communicate a non-worldly state. (11)

A single sattvic cognition arises, consisting of a collective apprehension (samūhālambana) that penetrates the stable emotions (sthāyibhāva) as they are intertwined with the three types of mental states (bhāva). 12.
In the very next moment, it necessarily manifests supreme bliss;
some teachers consider that [bliss] itself to be the aesthetic flavor (rasa), while others know that [manifestation] alone to be the rasa. //13//
Each of those individual cognitions is considered by them to be the cause;
the statement that "a stable entity is the rasa" is merely figurative. (14)

Since, in this way, no sequence is perceived due to the lack of interruption, this [type of suggestion] is known as *asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyadhvani* (suggestion where the sequence is imperceptible). ||15||

In Dhvani, the sequence between the expressed (vastu) and the embellishment (alaṅkāra) is to be inferred due to their intervention; therefore, they call this [type of] Dhvani "that in which the sequence between the indicated and the suggested is to be inferred. (16)

Because the aesthetic flavor (rasa), the emotion (bhāva), its semblance (tadābhāsa), the subsidence of emotion (bhāvaśānti), and so forth, necessarily manifest simultaneously in the immediately following moment without any temporal sequence. 17.

Defects such as those that are "ear-objectionable" (śrutiduṣṭa) and so forth are obstacles to rasa; their absence, too, is included within the causal complex [of aesthetic experience], as it effects the removal of what is undesirable. (18)
The styles (rīti), the qualities (guṇa), and the knowledge thereof are also causes; and the ornaments (alaṅkāra), when understood, become factors that bring about full development. (19)

The word, by means of its function in the form of suggestion (vyañjanā), is the communicator of that [suggestion], which makes known the qualities (guṇas), ornaments (alaṅkāras), styles (rītis), and poetic sentiments (bhāvas). 20.

The function of this word [‘Thou’], pregnant with bliss, consists in the immediate intuition of the effect [the Self], just like the function of the cognition arising from such sentences as “You are the tenth. ||21||
"Because of the scriptural statement, 'That indeed is the essence,' eternal bliss is manifested;
the realization of that self-luminous [reality] consists of the nature of non-conceptual bliss. (22)

As for the difference regarding the produced (*kārya*) and the indicated (*jñāpya*), etc., which has been described by some—that too should be applied according to this method, so as not to contradict the treatises. (23)
The scriptures declare that supreme bliss is indeed the Self, which is Rasa;
this has been demonstrated as the manner in which that [Rasa] is manifested through words. 24.

In the section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda), the Bhaṭṭas have stated that descriptions of forests, mountains, and so forth are for the sole purpose of providing pleasure to the hearers. (25)
Even in the theory that [the word] denotes "being connected with an action" (kāryānvitatva), there is no contradiction whatsoever;
for an action is desired as happiness precisely because it is what is sought by one who desires to act. (26)
But no evidence whatsoever is observed for an extraordinary injunction;
nor is it logical that all words in the world should have that as their primary purport. (27)
And the status of being a means of valid cognition consists in making known what was previously unknown and being purposeful;
moreover, the view that verbal testimony is directed solely toward action has been refuted by the Teachers themselves. (28)
By the logic of the "Deity-Topic" (Devatādhikaraṇa), even through words whose primary intent lies elsewhere, there arises a cognition of a purposeful, unknown, and uncontradicted object. (29)
Therefore, whether they are directed toward another meaning or possess independence, words manifest supreme bliss in accordance with their respective auxiliary factors. //30//

Thus ends the section titled "The Description of the Specific Types of Devotion" in the *Śrī Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*, composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the preeminent wandering ascetic teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācāryavarya*), renowned throughout the world, and independent in all philosophical systems (*sarvatantra-svatantra*).
